maintopic: QUESTIONS.
QUESTIONS.
speechtext:
Referring to the. return showing the total amount expended up to the date of the said return in connection with the enforcement of the Military Service Act-
How much has it cost per man to secure each soldier enrolled under tbs said Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext:
The total expenditure to date incurred in connection with the Military Service Act is $1,803,581.61. This total expenditure includes the expenditures incurred in connection with the publicity campaign, the Dominion police, printing, subsistence and travelling expenses of men ordered to report for duty, and travelling expenses of men ordered to report for medical examination.
The registration of Class I men under the Military Service Act is, to date, 397,671. Therefore the total cost per registrant is $4.54.
There have been 39,760 Class I men actually placed on service to date, but to estimate the cost of securing these men, by the simple process of dividing the total number of men now on service into the total expenditure in connection with the enforcement of the Military Service Act to date, would not give a true estimate of the cost of drafting such men, for the reason that the greater percentage of the expenditure shown above has 'been spent in organization, the results of which are only now bearing fruit. One may safely say that every man drafted in future will materially reduce the cost of securing a recruit. It may therefore be plainly seen that at the present time it is impossible to estimate the cost of securing a recruit under the Military Service Act.

speechtext:
The Minister of Militia and Defence stated the other day that the young men would not be taken from the farms until after those in the cities and towns had been called to report, but as a matter of fact young men

on the farm are being called to report right along. Is any provision being made whereby these young men will be allowed to return to the farm temporarily until the men in the cities and towns have been called out?

We are now endeavouring to arrive at some means whereby young men of this age who are in the midst of seeding operations, after reporting-it is necessary to report because otherwise the machinery would be complicated-shall be allowed to return to their farms for a couple of weeks to complete their seeding, and I hope arrangemenits to this end will be completed to-night.

Humphke, who had two sons liable to service under the Military Service Act, was arrested by the municipal chief of police and carried to Pembroke for having in his possession deer skins out of season under the provincial law and was held pending trial at Pembroke. The two young men who were defaulters, whether in their own minds they connected the arrest in any way with their default or not, did subsequently come forward and surrender themselves. There was no connection whatever between the two matters.

speechtext: The House resumed the debate on the motion of Hon. A. K. Maclean (Acting Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of Ways and Means (resumed from May 1).

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to address the House for the first time, I crave that indulgence which is always so readily granted to a new member when he makes his maiden

speech. The questions now before the House are so important and so far-reaching that those of us who are unaccustomed to parliamentary debate are encouraged to take the opportunity to express our opinions with a feeling of less timidity than we would otherwise entertain. It is not my intention, in fact it would be extremely presumptuous of me as a new member, to discuss the questions now before us at very great length, but permit me to say that in my humble judgment the Acting Minister of Finance deserves to be highly congratulated on the excellent Budget Speech which he delivered-the most comprehensive and most important Budget Speech ever delivered in the Parliament of Canada, and under the most momentuous circumstances that ever faced a finance minister of this country in presenting the annual financial statement. The new taxation imposed involves a number of new departures and is in many respects drastic, but, Sir, under the existing circumstances there is not a member of the House, there is not a loyal Canadian, who will not cheerfully accept the impositions called for and endeavour to meet them so far as he is able.
The assembling of Parliament annually for the granting of supplies is . a basic feature of our system of responsible government, and the procuring of ways and means wherewith to administer the public business imposes upon those charged with the affairs of government a serious and onerous obligation. If that is true in normal times, it is far more iso at a time like the present when such serious conditions confront us. The result of the financial operations of the year, as disclosed by the Acting Minister of Finance, seems to me to be quite satisfactory; that is to say, all the ordinary or civil expenditure of the country has been provided for, and there is available the sum of $55,000,000 to be devoted towards paying off the debt created by the war. In the debate which has so far taken place upon the Budget, as well as in the discussions which have occurred on other occasions since the opening of Parliament, two questions have been deemed by hon. members opposite to be of primary importance in dealing with the serious situation which the war has created: One consists of a demand for the removal of the duties on agricultural implements, and the other is founded on the cry that if men are taken from the farm food production will seriously suffer. With regard to the first, I cannot pretend to any expert knowledge as to the merits or demerits of the subject, and, therefore, I will not venture to discuss it. But I understand, and I have heard the statement made repeatedly here, that it has been, agreed that all matters of this kind should remain in abeyance until the war is over. So far as regards the denuding the farm of labour is concerned, all will admit that it is a serious proposition, but it must be remembered that a far more serious proposition is waiting to be disposed of: The Hun is at the gate, the very existence of our Empire is trembling in the balance, civilization and liberty are in jeopardy, and the call is for men, more men, and still more men. I admit that serious inconvenience, and even hardship, will be caused to many by the taking of able-bodied men from the farm, but, Sir, this is a time when all our people are called upon to make some sacrifice, and I do not apprehend that the consequences to farm operations, as a result of conscripting our manhood, will be as serious as some would like to make us believe. Even after all our young men of military age have been called to the colours, we know there will be a certain percentage who cannot conform to the physical standard required by the Military Service Act, and such persons will be available for work on the farm. Again, there are a great many men employed in non-essential industries in our large cities, and these I think could also be commandeered to some extent to do farm work. The objection has been raised by the practical farmers, " Oh, such men do not know how to do farm work." Even so, Mr. Speaker, we must endure the inconveniences and hardships involved, and solve the problem as best we can. The great problem that faces us, and which we must do our best to solve, is to do our utmost to send men overseas to beat back the invaders.
Sir, we know, and it is a matter of record, that, at the special session of Parliament held in 1914, regardless of political parties or affiliations, Parliament and people were unanimous in declaring that they were behind those men, to the last man and the last dollar, who first went forth to do battle for Canada in the allied armies. Those sons of Canada who have distinguished themselves as brave soldiers, in numerous battles-Courcelette, Vimy Ridge, and other scenes of carnage-were assured when they went to fight for Canada's cause that Canadians to a man would stand behind them; and those forty thousand brave sons of Canada who made the supreme sacrifice for their country, and are



now sleeping in Flanders .fields, died with the conviction that their death would be avenged, because they were told when they left home that Canada was behind them to the last man and the last dollar. Our friends on the opposite side appear to question or to demur as to whether they should enter into the matter of supplying men or of doing what is necessary, or at least of doing so with enthusiasm and spontaneity, for they say: "The Government did not do this and that thing as it should have been done; the Government have made mistakes; therefore why should we show any enthusiasm in rallying to their support now?" Let us see: suppose we admit that the Government has made mistakes. Is there any Government that has not made mistakes? Has the British Government not made many mistakes in this war, as it has made in some other .wars? The wonder to my mind is that Canada in this titanic undertaking has made so few mistakes. Canada had no knowledge, at least very little practical knowledge, of warfare. She knew little of recruiting men and making soldiers of them, or equipping and sending them to the scene of battle. She was engaged in peaceful pursuits, developing her great natural resources, when the war broke out. But, Sir, in face of all that, Canada did a marvellous thing when, within the space of a few weeks, she sent a flotilla of transports across the Atlantic carrying 33,000 trained Canadian soldiers who, but a few short weeks or months before, were all civilians. That is something for which Canada should get credit and of which she might well he proud. It is true that she has received encomiums. The United States, which had not then entered the war, that great nation, our last and greatest ally, of one hundred million people, say: We take off our hat, we bow to Canada for her extraordinary achievements in this war.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
Canada became a name to conjure with in Great Britain, in France, and on the continent of Europe in consideration of what she has done, and of what she is still doing, towards upholding her place, her dignity and her prestige in this struggle.
There is something else that Canada has done in consequence of the war which has brought her before the world in, I might say, an envious light. She has become a great financial country. Before the war, when Canada needed money, she went abroad to borrow it. But the time came

when it was very difficult, indeed next to impossible, for Canada to obtain money from other countries. She then turned to her own people, and you know, Mr. Speaker, the record of the loans that have been placed in Canada, the generous, enthusiastic, and overwhelming response Canadians have made by pouring their money and treasure into the coffers of the country for the purpose of carrying on the war. In this respect Canada has established herself among the nations in an important light, of which a few brief years ago we scarcely had any conception. Having done so much, it is our duty to continue in well-doing. When the Minister of Finance comes down to Parliament and asks for almost a billion dollars, there is no murmuring; every one is satisfied that this money must and shall be raised, and that that portion of it which it is necessary to raise by borrowing, apart from taxation, can be furnished by our people when the loans are issued, as has been done before. In view of all these things, we have reason to be proud of our country, and it is our duty to continue to make sacrifices even greater than those we have so far been called upon to make. The one thing necessary is to win the -war. For, Mr. Speaker, should we fail, should the Hun break through, what would be the good to us of our farms, or our money, or anything else we possess and cherish most dearly? The iron hoof of the invader's war horse would despoil our country; we would become serfs; civilization would be wiped from the face of our land, and freedom and constitutional liberty would be trampled under foot. God forbid that there should be any reason for believing that this will take place-but the possibility exists. Under these circumstances, Sir, is any sacrifice too great to be made by an honest, honourable land patriotic people? I have all along been convinced that a great many of us im Canada have not taken the war with sufficient seriousness. Look at the conditions across the Atlantic, in England, Scotland, prance, Belgium. No able-bodied men aTe found there; farming operations are carried on by women, old men and young boys. Yet iwe murmur if we are subjected to some inconvenience; if we are not allowed to carry on our farming and our fishing operations just as we have been doing all along. The venerable member for Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon) who addressed) the House the other night, desires that the fishermen shall be allowed to carry on their business until the 1st of September, when they wdll be will-

ing to enlist. In order that such a course should be of benefit to Canada, the hon. gentleman should have a conference with the Kaiser and ask him to restrain his forces until that time. That is the way these extreme proposals present themselves to me. However, I am satisfied that the men will be procured and that not such great inconvenience will be suffered by the farmers and fishermen as hon. gentlemen are disposed/ to conjure up. In any event, the winning of the war is the one and only grand and paramount object which we ought to have constantly before us.
Having said so much about the immediate question involved in the motion before you, Sir, I may be permitted to discuss a question which peculiarly affects the province from which I come. I refer to communication between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. Doubtless some of the older members of the House have often heard the complaint of members from Prince Edward Island; as a matter of fact, when the Island members made their statement regarding their disabilities in the matter of winter communication, the press used to say that it had been "Prince Edward1 Island day" in the House of Commons.. Sir, I shall not inflict any wail or complaint upon you, but I wish to give a brief history of the winter navigation of the etraits between. Prince Edward Island and the mainland. To many members of the House the subject may not be of particular interest, but it is. my duty to those whom I represent to raise my voice here with regard to the disabilities of Prince Edward Island, in the matter of railway facilities and winter communication.
It is a misfortune, perhaps., to live on an island. The people are necessarily shut off from other lands by water, and in northern latitudes, where the water congeals in winter, it is a serious, problem to be on an island. We are isolated, land, if I may play upon the word, we are and have been ice-olated during the winter. But if we have been isolated, and if we have been ice-olated, I think it cannot be said that we are insulated; that we come here with insular ideas, or are not sufficiently broadminded and magnanimous, to meet the views of our friends from the other provinces. It is said that people 'bom on an island sometimes have insular ideas, but I shall endeavour to show that I am not one of them, and that if there is- anything like that in my make-up, it is something over
87J
which I have no control and for which I cannot properly be held responsible.
On account of our ibeing in this isolated condition, the crossing of the straits, of Northumberland during winter has been a very serious, difficult and hazardous undertaking. During all the days before Confederation, this was our condition. Some gentlemen here to-day may have gone through the experience of crossing the Straits in winter, .the crossing being made in ice boats to which the passengers were, in a sense, harnessed with straps over their shoulders. They paid their fares* and worked their passages, too. Of course, under these conditions passenger traffic between the Island and the 4 p.m. mainland during the winter was not extensive; no one left during the winter season unless it was absolutely necessary for him to do so.
The first meeting to bring about the confederation of the provinces was held in Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, which may justly be called the cradle of Confederation. Curiously enough, when Confederation was consummated in 1867, Prince Edward Island did not join the union because she thought that the terms offered were not such as would meet her necessities, the crux of the difficulty being the' winter navigation of the straits. In 1873, however, when she thought the matter had been so arranged that there would be no further difficulty, Prince Edward Island, under what is known as the " better terms," becange a province of the Dominion. In order that we may have a fair understanding of one of the conditions which induced Prince Edward Island to become a member of the Confederation and which was cited in the bond, I quote these words from the Imperial Order in Council under which Prince Edward Island came into the Dominion of Canada:
Efficient steam service for the conveyance of mails and passengers to be established and maintained between the island and the mainland of the Dominion, winter and summer, thus placing the island in continuous communication with the Intercolonial railway and the railway system of the Dominion.
That was the condition that the people of Prince Edward Island desired the most. Prince Edward Island became a member of the Dominion of Canada in 1873. About three and a half years later, the first attempt was made to implement the above promise by putting the steamer Northern Light on the route between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. The Northern

the mainland should wait until times are better and money will be easier to obtain.
During the past winter, for the first time, the car ferry plied between Port Borden and Cape Tormentine, and the success that has attended its operations during a winter of unprecedented severity has revolutionized the ideas of the people of the island regarding their connection with the mainland. They now feel for the first time that they are a part of Canada, that they are not isolated as they had been in past years. Here is the proof. There was not a day during the winter that the car ferry could not cross in these heavy ice flows, and on some days it made two or three round trips. It is able to make the passage in fifty minutes under favourable circumstances, and at no time was it more than three hours in making the crossing. There was not a day upon which it might not have crossed, although there were a few days when it did not cross, because there were no trains on either iside and consequently nothing to cross for.
What we desire now is to have the Prince Edward Island railway standardized. We would like to see this work commenced as soon as possible, but no one realizes more fully than the people of Prince Edward Island that this is not a time when we should ask for extra appropriations when so much of our money is required to carry on the war. The standardization of the Prince Edward Island railway could be regarded in the light of a war measure. Prince Edward Island is an agricultural province, and it is extremely productive- in fact,, we have really no idea of the extent of its productivity-but if facilities are afforded for the transportation of the island's products it is capable of increasing its agricultural production at least a hundredfold. If that Ibe true, Sir, and if we can contribute that much more towards feeding the soldiers than we are now doing, would it not be sufficient ground for the Government undertaking the work of standardization without much delay? It is for the Government to say when that work -shall begin, but the people of the island would like to see it started forthwith. If that were done the output of Prince Edward Island's products would be augmented to such an extent that it would be by no means a losing speculation for the Government."
Let me give further reasons why, in our opinion, it would be wise for the Government to undertake this work now.. The operation of the narrow gauge car at present used costs about as much as the opera-
tion of the great car used on the Intercolonial railway, so that the improvement suggested would effect a saving there. Economies could also be brought about by a change in the system of handling produce. At present all freight shipped from Prince Edward Island goes to Port Borden, where it is transferred from narrow gauge to broad gauge cars, and then the cars are run on to the ferry and carried to the mainland. The cost of transferring freight in this way is from four to five thousand dollars a month. Now, taking the annual cost as $50,000 or $60,000, that amount capitalized would be equal to about $1,000,000, or, in other words, it would represent about one-half the cost of standardizing the road, as far as I am able to learn, in order to handle the increased volume of freight. Last year, owing to want of transportation, there were two million bushels of potatoes that could not be carried away from Prince Edward Island. More than that, the numerous steamships carrying freight from the island to other points-for example, to Newfoundland, Montreal, Boston and Halifax-have all, or nearly all, been eliminated owing to the abnormal conditions brought about by the war. As we all know, Mr. Speaker, almost any kind of vessel that is available is quickly picked up now for war transportation purposes, with the result that Prince Edward Island shipments are confined to the one route via Port Borden.
Another point arises in connection with the shipment of coal. In our province there are no coal mines, and coal has to be imported from Nova Scotia and other places. The volume of coal requiring to be transported by the car ferry, in addition to all the other products to which I have referred, represents something like forty thousand tons. There is this further point to be borne in mind: It is expected that Prince Edward Island, as a result of the campaign in favour of increased production, will this year have seeded some seventy-five thousand acres more. The product of that area, representing probably fifty-six thousand tons, will also need to be transported. All this great volume of freight, representing a total of something like 247,846 tons-calculating from the figures of last year's exports and taking into consideration the freight that was held up and could not be forwarded- will have to go by the car -ferry during the present year. The present export facilities will therefore not be adequate, and when they involve a transfer it means delay and an increased outlay of money.

I hope, Mr. Speaker, I am not wearying the House, tout even at the risk of doing so, I must present the case for my province.
I am talking on behalf of those who sent me here and who expect me to do my duty, and it is in the humble endeavour to discharge that duty that I am making my plea to the House this afternoon.
In addition to the expenditures to which I have already referred it will cost, to begin with, probably four or five hundred thousand dollars to put the narrow-gauge railway as it now exists, into a condition for handling business this summer. Again, there is the further expense of transferring the freight, and handling the additional freight that will need transportation. These figures will indicate to you the extraordinary disadvantage from which Prince Edward Island is suffering at the present time; and in my opinion the improvements desired with the elimination of these extra costs would not involve such a large grant from the Federal exchequer as it would if none of these subsidiary conditions prevailed.
There are other items that might be introduced to swell present expenses. There are, for example, the claims against the Government which may be brought any day arising out of the loss of potatoes and other perishable goods owing to the failure of the narrow-gauge railway to move them from the Island. Adding all the items together, I estimate $936,409 a%.the amount which the Government stands called upon to pay under present conditions.
There are other reasons why the people of Prince Edward should have the railway gauge broadened and its standardization commenced. They are reasons which will be beneficial to the Dominion, and to Prince Edward Island especially. During the past winter, it cost $67,000 to fight the snowstorms blocking the road, which had to be shovelled out. Every one acquainted with railways will understand that with a broad gauge and more powerful engines the snow blockade could toe better handled and its inconvenience reduced to a minimum at a much smaller cost.
There is the movement of certain perishable products also to be considered. In addition to toeing a great agricultural province, the richest and most abundant fisheries abound on our coast. The fresh fish industry would secure the best results from the quickest possible transportation to the markets on the mainland. If the beautiful fish that we catch on the coast of Prince Edward Island could be shipped from there
in the morning and brought into Montreal, for instance, the next morning, fresh from the sea, would that not be something worth working for? Prince Edward Island would benefit by it, and certainly other parts of Canada would not lose by it. There are other perishable products which should get to the markets in the shortest possible time and in the best possible condition. We have no hope that this ever can be done until we have the gauge standardized. Standardization will come some time; we have got so far ahead now, and the conditions that I have laid down seem to me to be of sufficient force to be some inducement to the Government to take up the work at as early a date as possible. Altogether, apart from the sentimental question, there is no longer any doubt in Prince Edward Island about the feasibility of practical daily communication, winter 1 and, summer, between the island and the mainland. The problem involved in the winter navigation of the straits is solved, and we feel that, at least, we have taken the first and greatest stride forward towards being really part of Canada. We no longer feel ourselves isolated. We only wish the completing of the railroad standardization to make our railroad situation as that of any other part of Canada, and to enable us to ship our products from any part of the Island to any part of North America without breaking bulk, and that any passenger boarding a train on the Island will not be obliged to leave his car until he reaches his destination. These are reasons which appeal to us, and I wish I was sufficiently persuasive to convince the Government that now is the time to standardize the Prince Edward Island railway. If I could convince them, I feel sure that within a short time the work would be commenced.
I do not know that I shall trespass upon your patience any further, Mr. Speaker, unless to thank you very sincerely for the generous hearing that has been accorded to me, upon*these matters so dear to the hearts of the people of Prince Edward Island, the first time that I have risen in Parliament to address you.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Mclsaac) who has just taken his seat will pardon me if I do not follow him very much in the speech which he has just made. If I had any criticism to make of his speech, it would be that he was lacking, like some of us, in terminal facilities, in knowing where to stop. The

great difficulty of the hon. member was where to begin. He began away too far back; if he had begun at the end of the railroad, as he should have begun, he would have been through with his business long ago. But, of course, when the hon. gentleman makes his next speech he will know better where to begin, and he will be shorter and more to the point. He will learn, of course, that if he desires to tell us that the sun is in the heavens, that the sea has its 'boundaries, and thait they will not trespass them; that there is light and darkness-he can tell us these things without going back to Genesis and saying that the Lord crealted the heavens and the earth in a certain set number of days. Some of these things could have been taken for granted, and it would have shortened his time a good deal. However, there is great latitude to be given to men who speak for the firslt time in the House of Commons, and I rather congratulate my good friend on the way in which he presented his case.
Before il forget it, there is something else in connection with his speech which seems to be coming to us from that side of the House a great many times and from a great many members. It is this somewhat secretive agreement that was entered into some months ago evidently when the Union Government was formed. It was first mentioned in this House some three or four weeks ago by the hon. member for Brantford (/Mr. Cockshutt) who made the open statement that there was such an agreement. There was no denial of it, except that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Crerar) was in his seat and I noticed that he ominously shook his head, which I took to be a disagreement with the hon. member's statement. However, the country had the advantage of hearing the statement of the hon. member for Brantford, but they did not see the Minister of Agriculture shake his head. So the statement of the hon. member goes uncontradicted. Last night we heard a revival of that atement by the hon. member for 'Springfield (Mr. Richardson) who told us again that there is such an agreement, and from his remarks we would gather that he is a party to it himself. To-day, the hon. member for King's, P.E.I. (Mr. Mclsaac), has once more stated that there is such an agreement. There are people in this country who would regard an agreement of that kind as unconstitutional and unparliamentary.
In dealing with public questions, representatives of the people in this House are flMr. McKenzie.]
supposed to be free agents, to be governed by the facts put before them, and it is at , variance with the principles of proper representation that members should come into the House like sheep going to market, their legs tied and their heads in a bag, and do exactly what they are told. If they venture for a moment to differ from the course laid down for them, this agreement is pointed out to them. Some day an hon. gentleman on this side may move that this agreement be brought down-for, of course, we have every reason to believe that it is actually in existence. It will ibe interesting to learn when it was made and who are the parties to it.
I realize that any criticism we make of the Budget and of the Government should be sane, serious and well-founded, and that nothing be said that savours of a desire to impede the progress of the Government in the steps which it is taking to deal with the serious question now confronting the country. I think I may safely say that no criticism of an unfair kind has been made from this 'side of the House. I congratulate the Acting Minister of Finance upon the mechanical paTt of his speech-as to its style, construction and delivery-and, so far as it is consistent with the position I take,
I congratulate him also upon his success in presenting to the House a very difficult and a very bad case. The hon. gentleman has disappointed some of his friends outside of the House by the ability he has
5 p.m. shown in dealing with this very important matter. The Journal-Press, the special organ of the Prime Minister in this city, has, of course, a monopoly of the brains of this country and of the foresight and thought of the city of Ottawa. It is said that the editor of that great journal is in close touch with the Prime Minister, by whom he is guided in the more intricate and difficult questions with which 'he has to deal. Picking up this newspaper two or three weeks ago, I noticed that in an outburst of wisdom the Journal-Press had declared that surely the Prime Minister would not entrust such a very serious task as the delivery of the Budget speech to the incapable hands of the member for Halifax. For the sake of Nova Scotia and of auld lang syne, I am glad that the Acting Finance Minister has acquitted himself in such a way as to demand that the Journal-Press apologize and take back its gratuitous opinion of his capacity. We assure the hon. gentleman that whatever hie friends over there may think of him, we on this side

etill have a lingering regard for him and hold a good opinion of his ability to deal with such important matters as have been dealt with in the Budget. Of course, in the minds of evilly-disposed persons there is a doubt as to the paternity of this speech. It is said that the speech was born in the United States of Canadian parents; that the hurried visit of the Prime Minister to New York recently was for the purpose of smuggling this infant into Canada and handing it over to the hon. gentleman who has presented it for christening to the House. Personally, I do not believe that. In any case, I give the Minister of Finance credit at least for not having written that part of it which refers to his own excellence and to all the wonderful things that he has accomplished.	'
Having said that much about the style and character of the Budget speech, a conscientious and God-fearing man like myself cannot say anything further in praise of it. The ridiculous suggestion is made that we have a surplus. That fallacy, that heresy, has been running through the speeches of the Minister of Finance ever since the war broke out. We always had a surplus in one part of the account and a deficit of some millions in another. The Acting Minister of Finance should not have been induced to incorporate in the Budget speech the statement that we had a surplus. To say that we had a surplus on ordinary expenditure might be tolerated. If since the war began we had continued the same revenue, the same taxation, the same sources of income that we had when the war broke out; if we bad dealt only with ordinary expenditures and had something to the good, we might reasonably and with a fair degree of consistency say that we had a surplus on ordinary expenditure. But such is not the case. Immediately on the outbreak of war we levied war taxes. We levied business taxes, and we are getting money from stamps and from many other things which the minister mentioned in his Budget Speech. From the Business Profits War Tax the minister told us we are getting $21,271,283; from banks, $836,724.28; from insurance companies, $385,127.68; from trust and loan companies, $267,917.68; from inland revenue from railways, steamships, telegraph and cable companies, stamps, etc., $2,229,922.81; making a total, according to the speech of the minister, of $24,990,975.45. Besides those taxes which the minister has specified, there was the flat 7J per cent extra duty which was placed upon the whole trade of every kind and description of the country. Possibly
the minister could not tell us exactly what that amounts to, but it would probably amount to somewhere around $25,000,000.
I am only guessing at the amount. At all events we have a specific tax of something like $50,000,000 or more, which we have collected from the people of this country as a special war tax. The minister has taken that $50,000,000 of special war tax, and he has applied it, with the rest of the revenue, to the ordinary business of the country, and then when he adds it all up, he does not put one cent of it to the credit of the war until he finds a surplus, and then, he says: We have a surplus. It is perfectly clear to the most ordinary person that this is not a fair nor an honest way of stating the account. When we have gone after the people for special taxes for war purposes, they should be credited to the war, and if you are going to deal with special accounts, they should be kept evenly balanced, having the one fairly meet the demands of [DOT]the other. When the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) in the past told us that we had surpluses, and when the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. A. K-. Maclean) to-day tells us that we have a surplus of $55,000,000, they are absolutely stating a case which is not fair, and which is not, so to speak, putting their cards on the table, and showing the people of this country exactly how the account stands. That is not dealing with us fairly, and we should have the account presented and stated just as it is, so as to let the Canadian people know exactly what they have to deal with. We, as representatives of the Canadian people, are willing to put everything we have into the pot in connection with war conditions, but on the other hand we have a perfect right, and it is the inalienable right of every taxpayer of this country, to know where every dollar goes and what is done with the moneys of the people. In the early stages of the war I remember well the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) making one of his eloquent speeches in this House, telling us that he, as a member of the Government, would begrudge the mis-spending of the moneys of the people for	anything
other than the purposes of the war. At that time, we expected that those words meant something, and that great care would be exercised in the expenditure of the moneys of the people in accordance with the true reason for which those extraordinary taxes were being collected. We are given part of the account, but we are not given all. It does not follow that, because our very hearts are set upon war

duties, and because every nerve is strained to do our full duty in the war, we mu-st be lax about other phases of our duty is representatives of the people, nor that the people of this country can be lax about the other branches of their business. If there ever was a time when proper care should be taken to safeguard every influence and opportunity for good and for the accumulation of wealth in this country, that time is the present. No advantage should be taken of the temper of the people and their feelings about expenditures, because in this time of war the people may not be as critical about expenditure as they otherwise would be. The closest attention should be given to expenditures, and we should know where every dollar goes.
This year there is a new departure in connection with some of the Estimates, and large amounts of money, that must come from the pockets of the people of this country for the purpose of carrying on the affairs of the country, are not being put into the ' Estimates at all in accordance with the old conditions. That is not right; that is not proper. If I should criticise the Government along those lines, I do so in accordance with my right as a representative of the people in this House. What is the good of sending men to this House unless they have a free hand and an open voice to place before you, Sir, and this country, what they regard as proper criticism and direction of the Government who, after all, ave but directors of the big concern of the people of Canada to carry on, in the best way, what they regard the will of the people to be? That is the position, and that is the way in which the business of the House should be conducted. I complain, I find fault with and I criticise the Government, and I bring that criticism as squarely as I can before the people, that the Government have no business to endeavour to get money in the thousands of dollars, much less in the millions, and possibly the hundreds of millions, without putting that expenditure before the House and having the members pass it with the ordinary conditions attached to- it as to how it shall be spent. That has not been done with the millions of dollars which we shall require for the purchasing of rolling stock and the operation of Government railways in this country. Why has that not been done? Is it because the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White), or the Government has no confidence in the people? Is it because they are afraid that hon. gentlemen in this House are not big enough and
[IMr. 'McKenzie.] [DOT]
broad enough and have not business ability enough to give them the money if it is properly required? And, are they afraid that we shall not place sufficient confidence in them- to allow them to spendi this money in the good old way? At all events we are, I am told, to pass an Act of Parliament by which we shall have nothing to say as to how, this money is to be spent. That should not occur, and free agent-s in this iHouse, whether they sit on the Government side or this side, should have something to say in the matter. We in this country are to-day in a condition when the people will no't stand for monopoly of that kind, whether that monopoly is exercised by the Government under Orders in. Council, or by concerns who have with the Government a pull which they should not have and which will perhaps induce and compel the Government to do things which they otherwise would not do. I submit that the temper of the Canadian people will not stand for that, and possibly we have stood too long for imposition of that kind. As far as expenditure,of railway money is concerned, it is not in the Estimates at all, and if my hon. friend took the moneys he will require out of this $55,000,000 alleged surplus, the whole amount 'would be wiped out and there would not be even a shadow of a surplus left. In order to show a surplus, he leaves this expenditure out of sight altogether; but he deceives nobody.
We had a lecturing address from the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) last night, and I have not been able to tell exactly on which side he is. He reminded me of the fellow who was perhaps a little under the weather and who asked, when out walking, "Which is the other side of the street?" A man told him "There is the other side of the street over there." The man went over, and when he got across asked another man, "Is this the other side of the street?" "No," said the man, "the other side of the street is over there." "Well," said he, "that man over there told me this was the other side of the street." The hon. member for Springfield, I think, is somewhat in that position; it is difficult for him to find which is the other side of the street. However, he wanted to criticise us and criticise the leader of the Opposition. Of course he had to criticise the railway policy of the present Administration; had a right to do that, and a very excellent field for criticism. I will not weary the House by going very far into these railway criticisms, but somewhat in answer to the

hon. member for Springfield, I must remind him that he has been in public life for a great many years. I have not the honour of his acquaintance, but I know he has been in this House before. He knows the history of the railway policies of the different parties in this country; how in 1903 the policy of my distinguished leader, the Bight Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, was launched in this country for the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and launched in no hole-in-the-comer way, but in the most open manner possible. Before a sod was turned or a dollar expended on that magnificent enterprise the people of this country were appealed to, and their verdict was given on the Government's policy in connection with that great enterprise. It is well known that in 1904 the battle royal from the Atlantic to the Pacific was between the railway policy of the then leader of the Opposition, now the Premier of this country, and the railway policy of the Laurier Government, and the verdict of the people was overwhelmingly in favour of my right hon. leader. Whatever else there may have been a division on there was practically not a dissenting voice on that policy from coast to coast. So that, as far as the railway policy of Sir Wilfrid Laurier is concerned and the course his Government took in connection with the railways of this country, he had the full sanction and approval of the people of this country. Again in 1908, after four years' work on the road, the people of Canada had the opportunity of passing judgment upon the railway policy of my right hon. leader again, and he was triumphantly returned to power. So satisfied were the people of Canada with his railway policy that during the campaign of 1908 the leader of the Opposition had really nothing to say about the railways at all. It was accepted by both parties that the proper course had been taken for the opening and development of this great country, of which we are all so proud and whose resources are so immense; it was this policy alone, within proper bounds, that was necessary to full discharge of the duty of any Government that might have been in power at the time. The difficulty is that new men have taken the wheel and are trying to work out the destinies of this country. Conditions which were all right in the hands of a master like the Premier of that day have become burdensome and too heavy to carry in the hands of people who do not understand the art of government as he did when he had control of the affairs of this country. The rod of empire has
fallen into hands which are not capable of wielding it in his masterful way, and the mole has become a mountain and the grasshopper a load. The new men are unable to carry these matters along, and the result is that the financial conditions in connection with the railways are such that the Government of the day, if I am to judge from their actions, will not dare to bring before the House the rea-l state of affairs in connection with railway matters. I would remind the hon. member for Springfield and the members generally who are supporting the Government that shortly after the Borden Government came into power in 1911 the Minister of Finance made his first speech in February of the following year. He was then, of course, fresh from his financing, fresh from the critical training which he had had as a financier, and anxious to discover any weak spots that could be found in the financial conditions of the country. There was a good deal of criticism then by newspapers supporting the Government of the railways the Government had on their hands at that time. If conditions were very bad, if there was anything that was dangerous to the finances of this country, or that might have a bad effect on the credit of this country I am sure the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) could very well have been entrusted with bringing that difficulty and weakness to the notice of Parliament and the country. Any person who wishes to see what he stated on that occasion can look up his speech. Of the financing of the country generally he spoke in glowing terms; he was delighted to find the country in such a prosperous condition, and glad that after every obligation had been properly met by the outgoing Government, that Government was able to hand over to him the sum of $40,000,000 to meet any fresh obligations that might arise; you will find that in his speech. He also said that while there was some criticism in connection with Grand Trunk Pacific, he was glad to be able to say that instead of that road being a burden or a debt on this country, it was a magnificent asset to the Canadian people.
That is the position as far as railway matters in this country were concerned at the time the Government of my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), whom I am pleased to follow, passed over the reins of power to hon. gentlemen opposite. If there is anything wrong, if things are not what they were at the time they took charge, it is their lookout. It is for them to see that

Yours sincerely, Wilfrid Laurier.
That offer was submitted to the Prime Minister in the early stages of the war. Why was not advantage taken of it? Was anything done by the Prime Minister to implement that offer? I am sorry to say nothing at all. The manner in which attempts were made to organize recruiting in Quebec has already been discussed several times, and the subject is not new, and what occurred is well known. If it was the intention of the Government to create dissension in Quebec and make recruiting a failure-and it was said that such was their intention-they could not have gone about it in a better way than they did. In most of the Canadian provinces our young men speak the English language, and they suffer no disadvantage from being trained by English instructors. But it is otherwise in the province of Quebec, where in large sections the population speak French exclusively. Not only the old people but the young folks use French entirely, and when it was a case of obtaining recruits it was hut natural to look for instructors who could make plain to these young men the requirements of the drill in their own tongue. Had there been a proper organization in connection with recruiting in the province of Quebec, men who could speak the French language, and who were in sympathy with the French people and understood their ways and their peculiarities, would have been placed at the head of that recruiting and in charge of the training of French Canadians.
What has happened? You would say at once: Surely they did that. Nothing of the kind. They sent men there to do recruiting, at least for the first two or three years, who did not know a word of French, and who were not of the same religion as those to whom they were sent. We cannot shut our eyes to the fact that we get closer to men who are of our own language and religion than we do to those who are not. I do not say that in a sectional way, or as finding fault with any man's language or religion; but these things are natural to us. As far as Quebec is concerned, men were sent there who were not in sympathy with the people on one or other of these very important phases of character, and the result was an absolute and a huge failure in re-

cruiting. That failure has been taken hold of by some men who wanted to start a sectarian fire in politics and use it to win the election. I sulbmit that if w-e had been playing politics and sectarianism with the Victory Loan the same result and the same failure would have followed that followed in Quebec recruiting when elements were introduced that were calculated to produce failure. I make these explanations on these statements to show that the Government of this country who Were in charge of the war 4id not always have the singleness of mind and heart which they wish other people to have to-day, and that they always and at all times had something else in view different to the winning of the war. There was no stage of the proceedings when they did not have the primary idea of politics and the winning of the election which was really a very heavy factor in whatever course they took in connection with these matters.
Having said that much on this question, I propose to give a little attention to some matters which came before the House, particularly last night, regarding the political situation and the policy of the different parties so far as the trade of this country is concerned. Let me assure you, Sir, that I do not propose to go very lengthily into these things, or to take up too much time. But it is well that we should always), whether we are Liberals or Conservatives, have a proper understanding of the faith and doctrine of our party and the principles for which we stand. If we lose that, if we have not the proper chart and compass upon what we stand for, and what we toelieve our party to stand for, we lose the full force and effect of the service which a party is supposed to render in the Government of a country. For, after all, partyism is an institution in this country; we have two parties, Liberals and Conservatives, and whether the Government is good or bad, whether the system is good or bad, it is still the system, and I must submit as my own opinion that, so far, it is the best system of governing that we have yet found. If we are going to have clean administration and proper cheeks one on the other, we must have a Government party and an Opposition party, and I wish to remind hon. gentlemen of the fact that in any province in this, or any, country, where there is an admixture of parties, and a forgetting of the responsibilities, rights .and privileges of parties, there has been corruption and a falling off in proper

administration, much to the loss of the people. For that reason,, if we are to recognize party government, we should have the best possible party government, and each party should take pride in its doctrines, ideas and traditions. Belonging, as I do, to the Liberal party, I am proud of its traditions and history, and I wish to keep it as much as possible unsullied from anything that might tarnish it, or stain the names of the great men who have been in the past and are to-day its leaders, or which would interfere in any way with the doctrines which we have always espoused as a party. The hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) last night endeavoured to mix things up and to lead the House and the country to understand that the Liberal party was not true to its principles and to its professions as set forth in the platform of 1893, three years before the Liberal party took over the Government of this country in 1896.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

That is the view which Sir George Foster, Sir Robert Borden and* Sir Charles Tupper took of the difference between the policy of the Liberal party and the policy which they advocated when they were in power, their policy being better known and understood as the National Policy. It is only fair to the House and to the Liberal party at this stage of our history that I should again remind the House of what the policy of the Liberal party was in 1893. These are the ten planks of the famous platform of the Convention of 1893:
1.	That the customs tariff of the Dominion should be based, not as it is now, upon the protective principle, but upon the requirements of the public service; that the highest interest of Canada demands a removal of this obstruction to our country's progress toy the adoption of a sound fiscal policy which, while not doing injustice to any class, will promote domestic and foreign trade and hasten the return of prosperity to our people; that to that end the tariff should be reduced to the needs of honest, economical and efficient Government; that it should be so adjusted as to make free or hear as lightly as possible upon the necessaries of life, and should toe so arranged as to promote free trade with the whole world, more particularly with Great Britain and the United States.
2.	That the Liberal party is prepared to enter into negotiations with a view to obtain a fair and liberal reciprocity, including a well considered list of manufactured articles.
3.	That the Convention deplores the gross corruption in the management and expenditure of public moneys.
4.	That we cannot hut view with alarm the large increase of the public debt and of the control of the annual expenditures of the Dominion and the consequent undue taxation of the public, under the Governments that have been continuously in power since 1878, and we demand the strictest economy in the administration of the Government of the country.
5.	That it is the ancient and undoubted right of the House of Commons to inquire into all matters of public expenditure and into all charges of misconduct in office against ministers of the Crown.
6.	That in the opinion of this Convention the sale of public lands of the Dominion should toe to actual settlers only and not to speculators upon reasonable terms of settlement, and in such areas as can be reasonably occupied and cultivated by the settler.
7.	The repeal of the Franchise Act, that we should revert to the provincial franchises.
8.	To make the House of Commons a fair exponent of public opinion and to preserve the historic continuity of counties, it is desirable that the conformation of the electoral division,
[iMr. McKenzie.]
county boundaries, should be observed, so that in no case no parts of different counties could he put in one electoral division.
As regards the ninth plank, I am not sure that these are the exact words, but this is the substance of it:
9.	That the policy In regard to appointments to the Senate of Canada should he revised and brought forward in conformity to certain public opinion.
10.	That, whereas public attention is at present much directed to the consideration of the admittedly great evils of intemperance, it is desirable that the mind of the people should be clearly ascertained on the question of prohibition by means of a Dominion plebiscite.
In moving that resolution, the right hon. gentleman who now leads the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) made the following observations, which form a small section of the speech that he delivered to the Convention on that occasion:
I say the policy should be a policy of free trade such as they have in England-
That is, he says, it should be.
-That, I am sorry to say that the circumstances of the country cannot admit at present of that policy in its entirety, tout I speak to you from this day forward that it should fie the goal to which we aspire. I propose to you from this day forward, although we cannot adopt the policy itself, to adopt the principle which regulates it; that is to say, that though it should be your misfortune for many years to come to have to raise the revenue toy customs duties, those duties should be levied only so far as is necessary to carry on the business of the Government. Nothing is more difficult-that is one of the evils of protection-than to wipe away protection because under it interests have been established, which every man who has at heart the interest of all classes must take into consideration. It is always easy to increase the tariff because toy doing so you increase the private fortunes of certain individuals, but whenever you decrease the tariff it has always to be done with careful consideration, and I am sure that when the Liberals are in power they will not be in different to this primary truth.
I have quoted the particular part of the speech which dealt with the character of that policy. It was clearly laid down at the time that, although the goal of the Liberal party was to be free trade, it could not be accomplished at one bound, but that the Liberal party hoped to go forward from step to step and to adopt freer and freer trade from time to time as that could be accomplished without any deterrent to or interference with vested interests in this Country. I need not tell hon. members, who are familiar with the progress of the country the rapid strides that were made under the administration of the right hon. gentleman and how this country

prospered under that policy and under the management of it by himself and the wise men whom he gathered around him to compose his government. It is unnecessary to point out how, under his administration and under his policy, population rapidly flowed into this country,
The great West, which is of course the great hope of this country, has developed and expanded so that villages have become towns and towns cities, and those vast territories' which were practically unorganized at the time the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) took office were flourishing provinces before he left power, and rapidly coming into a position where they could vie with the older provinces of the Dominion. Those were the conditions brought about by the policy of the Liberal party, and that is the policy which we want to keep to the fore all the time. We have no thought of departing from the policy which we followed when in power. When we return to power again we hope to bring happiness, prosperity and honest administration to this country, and we shall not be called upon to depart from that good old basic old rock of the constitution of the party, on which we have built for so long, and built so well.
The hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) hinted last night (that he did not know where the Liberal party was; he did not know whether there were any of that party still alive. He need only look across the floor to see a very sturdy section of them left, and if he will go to the country to-morrow, stripping his platform of this cry about the war, the cry by which the people have been falsely and improperly divided, if he will appeal to the country on a clean, straight -administration and the best policy for the people in peace times, he will find out where the people are, and whether there is any of the Liberal party left.
Referring once more to the development of this country under the regime of my right hon. leader up to his going out of power in 1911, what is the testimony and what are the declarations not only of his friends but of his. political opponents as to what he achieved in the glorious period during which he had charge of the affairs of this country? When we declared for reciprocity in 1911, what was the slogan of the then leader of the Opposition? From the Atlantic to the Pacific his appeal was: The policy which has been in force for the last fifteen years has brought this country to such a high mark of success, the country
is in such a magnificent state of prosperity that it would be folly and a sin to interfere with present conditions. Let well enough alone; Sir Wilfrid Laurier with his immigration policy, his tariff policy, his expenditures of the revenues of this country, and everything that goes to the making up of a successful administration and a growing country, has done well; we' have no fault to find; let us stand by the policy of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and leave well enough alone. That was tlhe appeal made on every hustings by the then leader of the Opposition. He did not recognize that it was well enough; it was very good, and a magnificent departure from the conditions he found when he took office. Then the country was bankrupt. There was not enough revenue collected to meet the ordinary expenditure. One province was flying at the throat of another, and there were dissensions and dissatisfaction between men of different religious creeds-. But Sir Wilfrid Laurier came into power, and brought this country into the harmonious and happy condition it was in in 1911.
We have a magnificent territory, extending from ocean to ocean. Our resources are just as good as those of the United States -and we have a territory that is wide and comprehensive, and capable of receiving and looking after something like one hundred millions of people, but to-day we have only got seven millions, what was the vision of that great statesman? Am I to sit here, he asked, with -a territory around me capable of making homes for one hundred or one hundred and fifty -million people and foe satisfied with only seven million people? Is it not my duty as the responsible head of this Government to provide -such means as will make 'Canada a happy and contented country, an inviting country for people to live in? And he started out to make Canada a place where there would he open markets, where the man who was settled on the land would have right at his door a ready market for whatever he raised. Although the English market was very good, it was three thousand miles away, and you h-ad to send your goods by rail to a steamer, and then by steamer across the Atlantic, and then perhaps by rail for a further distance. The English market was good, but it was not natural and proper to ship to that market when we had right by our side some one -hundred and ten million of people, speaking our own language, and requiring the things we produced. Would it not have been better and more reasonable to sell our products to them, where we could get the



best price, than to send them to the English market three thousand miles away? Was not that the proper course for the Government to take? That was the policy which Sir Wilfrid Laurier placed before the people at that time with a view to making Canada an inviting place for the millions of people for whom we had room, and who would no doubt have come to this country if reciprocity had been accepted. But there were people in this country whose interests were being interfered with. As was said by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) the other night, there was a Diana of the Ephesians in this country; the profits and trade of certain people were likely to be interfered with if the national barriers against trade between Canada and the United States were broken down. There was enough force brought to bear on that occasion to defeat us, not squarely and honestly, but through raising the cry of disloyalty and traitorism. The flag was waved and the question was asked, " Under which flag will you live? ft is well enough to have trade, but we must stand by the flag." But those days have gone by, and now everybody who has any proper conception of national development can see that that would have been the best course for this country to pursue. Friends of the Government and the Government themselves, one after the other, are. forsaking the props and pillars that supported them at that time, and everything that we advocated in connection with the trade relations between the two countries is about to Ibe adopted; at least they are making a show of doing it, whether they mean it or not. It is pretty hard to know sometimes whether they are going or coming, because they try to make every circumstance suit their whims and caprices. At one time they put Ontario against Manitoba, and at another some other province against another section of the country, just as it suits them for the time being. We have evidence enough of that. On 3rd December last, a certain policy was good enough for them, but now it has been changed for the time being; there is now a new fiddle and a new tune, but they will find out that the people of this country will not change the tune as rapidly as the Government think they ean do in matters of the gravest consequence with which they have to deal.
I have outlined the course which my right hon. leader has followed since he laid	down his broad
platform in 1898, and the policy upon which he came into power in 1896
['Mr. McKenzie.]
under which he administered the affairs of this country so grandly and magnificently up to 1911 and upon which, in its advanced state, he gloriously went out of power m that year.
I said in the early part of my remarks that it was important for every man, if he belonged to a party, to do what he could to keep that party clean, strong and devoted to the best interests of the country. Let me remind the House that although we had fifteen years of office, although we had handled millions of money in dealing with every kind of public enterprise, service and work in the country, we -went out of office in 1911 and every possible investigation was thrown after to discover where we had done -anything wrong. It is the proud boast that we can make to-day that although every department of Government was rifled from one corner to the other, not only with such men as they could employ in that work in Ottawa but with men brought from the Old Country to investigate the books of the department in the effort to find some scandal, no scandal was found. It was not shown t-hait one fifty cent piece was misappropriated in the fifteen years when we were in power. I do not like scandal-mongering and I am not a scandal-monger but I wish to remind the hon. gentleman of the conditions under which they went oult of power in 1896 and ask them to compare the conditions of those days with the conditions under which we handed over the reins of Government when it was our duty to do so in conformity with the views of the people.

speechtext: I think my hon. friend is misrepresenting the facts, unintentionally, no doubt. If he will examine the report carefully he will se'e that 5 cents is the margin, not the profit. The profit was considerably less than one cent.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
I will adopt the language of the minister and say it was a margin. The company took umbrage at Mr. O'Connor's report that they had even a margin of 5-05 cents, and immediately asked for another court. What did that court find? It did not find that they made a profit of 5 cents, but a great deal more than 5 cents. The company would not give Mr. O'Connor the necessary information to ascertain the difference between gross and net profits, so Mr. O'Connor figured it out from the overhead expenses of other companies and reached the conclusion put forth in his report. He found there was a margin of 5-05 cents. But what is that compared with what was found by the court that was appointed to whitewash Sir Joseph Flavelle, in the expectation that it would find that Mr. O'Connor was absolutely wrong and that there was no such margin. I have in my hand the report signed by Mr. Henderson, Mr. Brodie and Mr. Clarkson, the three gentlemen who were appointed to review the investigation of Mr. O'Connor and to report. It is only necessary for me to read the first section of their finding, as all I am concerned about is: Did they find that the profit was greater or less than 5:05

cent, as represented by Mr. O'Connor. Let me point out that Mr. O'Connor finds that on the turn-over, that is, in the handling of that particular quantity, there was a gross profit of the amount he mentions, but as I understand it, that does not include plant and overhead expenses generally, such as the land upon which the building stands and the machinery used in a business of this kind. I do not understand that Mr. OConnor figures on that at all. I think he simply deals with buying the goods and the turning over of them without any reference to the value of the stores, land, horses, engines or stock that the man might own. But what do Mr. Henderson and his commission find? They find that there is not only 5 per cent on the turnover but that the profits made by the companies during the war, were excessively high and yielded an extraordinary return on the capital investment. They say that in the year 1916 the trading profits of the Davies Company- that is iSir Joseph Flavelle-equalled eighty per cent on the company's investment in packing houses, plants, retail stores and everything else in connection with the business. Eighty per cent upon land, upon buildings, upon horses, upon engines, upon every conceivable thing they had in connection with the business. That is the finding of Mr. Henderson. It is plain, simple, clear and easy to be understood.
I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that there iwas no ground or justification given before the commission, of which Mr. Henderson was the head, for the appeal from the findings of Mr. O'Connor. I wish to bring this matter to the notice of the minister and to tell him in the most particular way that the people of this country think it was only because of the pull that this man, Sir Joseph Flavelle, and those who were associated with him in making these *huge fortunes, have with the minister and the Government- generally that has influenced them, and that it is only this hydraulic pressure that has lifted this man O'Connor out of office and thrown him on the street. That is the belief of this country and I submit that there is some fair *ground for it. From the day that he found fault with this man, Sir Joseph Flavelle, to this, in so far as the office of the Minister of Labour is concerned, it appears that there was no continuing city for him any more and that he could no longer live in comfort there.

But the manoeuverings and dealings of this great concern did not end with making eighty per cent out of the poor people of this country by reason of the fact that Sir Joseph Flavelle had the inside track, by reason of the fact that Sir Joseph Flavelle, through his influence, or his friendship with this Government, managed to secure a contract with the Imperial Government which no other concern could get. He could lose nothing no matter how much he paid. He had a contract with the Imperial Government that he would get a certain percentage on his buying price whatever it might be. There are hon. gentlemen sitting in front of me who know something about buying and they know that if they can go through the country with the knowledge that, whatever they pay, they cannot lose any money, and that if another man has not such a contract he cannot compete with them at all. A man, if he expects to make a few dollars, or a few cents, on his bargain, must buy at a certain price (because he knows what he has to sell for. Sir Joseph Flavelle was in the fortunate position that if he bought at ten cents he knew that he had a margin beyond that and if he bought at twelve cents his margin was the same. If the market went up by twenty, thirty, forty, or fifty per cent, he could not by any possibility lose. Together with that he had access to transports which enabled him to send his goods over to the other side and make profits on the turnover there through agencies to which he attached his machinery and he went on dealing and working and squeezing money out of the poor people of this country without any check or interference whatsoever. As one of the representatives of the people of this country, I maintain that there should be a check on conduct of this kind. The Government should have known what was going on in this business and this man should not have been permitted to make these extraordinary profits out of the life blood of the poor people of this country. This is a fair subject for comment and it should be brought to the notice of the Government and of the people. I do not think that I should apologize, or feel that I am imposing upon you, Sir, or upon hon. members, in bringing a matter of such vast importance to the notice of the only tribunal in the world with which we have anything to do that can remedy matters of this kind.
There is one thing more. Sir Joseph Flavelle was not satisfied with what he had done in connection with the investigation that took place, but, before I leave

that I venture to submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that it is a most extraordinary thing that although this man has been found guilty by Mr. O'Connor of extraordinary profiteering, and although Mr. O'Connor says that if this had been done while the Order in Council was in force, he would have regarded it as his duty and obligation to bring the matter to the notice of the Attorney General with a view to prosecution, no action was taken. If the minister discovered that this prosecution could be brought about by just making this Order in Council, which was produced with such a great flourish of trumpets, retroactive, by just changing the date from the twentieth to the first of the month, why did he allow this man, who was a criminal and who was robbing the people of this country, to escape punishment? If he were a cobbler he would have no show for his life, but this millionaire, this multimillionaire, a friend of this Government, the godfather Of the hon. Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) and who has a lease evidently on everything that is powerful and strong about this Government, can do as he likes and smile at any person who may suggest that he is injuring the country and discrediting its Government. I make these somewhat extraordinary and strong charges in the hope that I may stir up the Minister of Labour a little bit and that he may get on his cobbler armour and go after the man who has millions and who has great strength in this country and that he will give the country to understand, the poor as well as the rich, that there is only one King, one Government, and one line of justice for every man whether he be rich or poor. It remains for the Government to satisfy the people that that is the way things should be done. If they leave this matter as it is now and let this man escape with his eighty per cent, his millions and hundreds of millions, this man who was enabled to make five millions in less than six months out of the life blood of this country, I do not think that it will be regarded as wholesome for the Government or for any person who may be supporting them particularly in this zone where this disclosure has been so keenly felt.
In the city of Winnipeg only the other day we had an investigation into the conduct of this same man and his agencies in that part of the country. Food of the most delicate character, food that is not easy to get, to the extent of thirty-five tons of chicken, I understand, was allowed to rot in a certain cold storage in Winnipeg.
It was allowed to go to decay and had to be thrown out upon the dump rotten rather than sell it to the poor people of Canada at half a cent a pound less than the ordinary high price out of which these millions were being made as I have already stated. The Government appointed a Commission of Inquiry and this is what the commission says. But before I read its findings, let me say that it is sad to think that on a question of fact you cannot believe those people. You cannot believe Sir Joseph Fla-velle, I am. sorry to say, on a mere bald question of fact. He swears before Mr. Justice Meredith or Mr. Justice Duff, that certain work was being done for them for nothing, that it was being done absolutely free. We find his hand to an agreement according to which, in connection with identically the same work, he was getting five per cent on a million, or at least his company was getting five per cent on hundreds of millions of money. This man has spent a million dollars a day, the money of the Canadian people, three hundred millions of money a year, if not more, and a large slice of that was going through this company and somebody was getting five per cent. We would like to know how much it was.
