Very good, I say .that they are getting it, and that is what they are after. That is why a paper like Saturday Night is making an investigation and letting daylight into this, matter, to see that the people of this country are protected. If it can be shown that there is nothing wrong about this transaction, well and good. It is no business of mine, and if the transaction turns out to be honest and above board no person will be more pleased than myself. On the face of it, however, it looks as if this man was making a statement that does not square with the facts as they develop afterwards. If that is not so all right, but, as I understand it, his statements are not borne out.
As. to a question of fact, I have here the report of an officer, I presume appointed either directly or indirectly by the Government, in which the finding appears that a certain transaction of the William Davies Packing Company in Winnipeg was far from proper, and that the statements made in connection with the conduct of their business there are far from the truth. Now, Sir, there is no use in going half way with this matter, and I must ask your indulgence while I read to you a report:
J. D. McGregor, Esq.,
Western Representative,
Canada Food Board,
Winnipeg-, Man.
Dear Sir :
I received your letter dated March 14th, 1918, instructing me to hold, an investigation into the cold storage business of the William Davies Co. of the city of Winnipeg, with particular reference to the destruction recently of a large amount of poultry at the city incinerator.
After careful consideration I beg to report as follows:

Meetings of the Commission for taking evidence were held on the following dates: March 18th, 19th, 20th, 2ilst and 2'3rd, of 1918. On the morning of the 20th an inspection was made of the plant.
Mr. Isaac Pitblado, K.C., and Mr. A. E. Bowles, were counsel for the William Davies Co., and Mr. C. E. Finklestein for the Canada Food Board. They were present at all meetings.
All witnesses were duly sworn and evidence taken under oath.
I enclose herewith the transcript of the evidence taken before me, together with Exhibits filed.
In the following findings I refer to the pages of the evidence. I take it from your letter that while you wished me to deal with and recommend upon collateral matters arising therefrom yet you desired me to investigate and report upon the following two points in particular:
1.	Was there any "hoarding" of food?
2.	What was the cause of the deterioration of the poultry?
Mr. Karl Symonds, Manager of the plant of the William Davies Co. of Winnipeg, swore that the Head Office at Toronto knew nothing of his purchasing the poultry but he bought them "off my own bat" (Page 41). He did not at any time report having this quantity of poultry on hand to the Head Office, but he reported daily temperatures of the room in which they were held. He further swore that he gave instructions to his travellers to, sell "regardless of cost*' (Page 23). He swore "no price was set to Williams," one of his travellers (Page 23) that his instructions to sell "regardless of cost" were for the whole of the summer of 1917 (Page 33) that he never fixed the minimum price (page 104) that he instructed his travellers to meet alll competition (Page 35). On being recalled the following day he again swore that he gave instructions to seil "regardless of cost" (Pages 103 and 105).
Now that is the evidence of the manager, now comes the evidence of the travellers to whom he refers:
Symonds' evidence was contradicted by the evidence of his own two travellers, Messrs. E. A. Williams and F. D. Cundell.
E.	A. Williams swore Symonds did not instruct him to sell "regardless of cost" (Pages 261 and 26'6) swore that he, Williams, had an offer from John Campbell at the General Hospital at 19c and Williams phoned Symonds who instructed him not to sell at less than 20c (Page. 262).
F.	D. Cundell, also a traveller of the Davies Company, swore that Symonds did not instruct him to sell "regardless of cost" (Pages 271272) was not told that he had to undersell and get rid of it (Page 271) ; had to sell according to set price (Page 277) ; could have sold if price had been reduced (Page 272).
In addition to the evidence of the manager, Mr. Symonds, and the two travellers of the Davies Company, several quite disinterested parties gave evidence before me to which I give the utmost weight and to which I now refer. Mr. T. J. Coyle, broker, swore that Symonds offered him 20,000 pounds of poultry August 22nd, 1917, at 20 cents per pound. He wired order to Gunn-Langlois, Montreal, but they would not accept at that price. He swore Montreal firm would have purchased if

price was reduced, and that if Symonds had had a standing order with him to sell regardless of cost he could have sold the poultry.
John Campbell, Steward of Winnipeg General Hospital, swore that Davies Company refused to sell at market price, in October, [1917. He swore that he offered 19c. to Williams, the Company's traveller quoted 20c. and says he got some fowl from Swifts and Gordon Ironsides at 19c. during the month of October, 1917. He swore that Williams told him there was no fowl for sale in December, 1917, and January, 1918.
John Guest, Manager meat department, T. Eaton Co., swore Eatons could have sold the poultry, says he would have purchased it in January, February and March, 1919, at 20c.
W. D. Haight, produce Manager, Gordon, Ironsides and Fares, swore he could have sold chicken in January, February and March, 1918.
James Gallagher, President Gallagher, Holman and LaFrance, swore he disposed of a carload in Montreal to William Clark in December, 1917, at 21c.
At this point I should state that the evidence submitted by the Winnipeg branch of the Davies Company was to the effect that the poultry in question, amounting to 70,000 pounds was put in cold storage in their Winnipeg plant during the months of October, November and December of 1916.
In March, 1918, about one year and five months later, 50,000 pounds still remained, and it was found thar a large portion of it had deteriorated and 8,500 pounds was sent to the city incinerator for destruction. The W. Davies Company have been instructed and are rapidly disposing of all stock on hand that are fit for food at very reduced price and there will be about 1,500 and 2,000 pounds more to be destroyed out of the balance in storage.
A comparison of prices for storage poultry as shown in Gordon, Ironsides and Fares price list and Cundell's price list will show that the prices of Cundell, traveller for Wm. Davies Co., run slightly higher all through the year 1917 for both fowl and chicken.
The commissioner has added a table here which shows that the prices of the William Davies Company all through are higher than those of Gordon, Ironsides & Fares. In June, 1917, he says that Gordon, Ironsides & Fares quoted fowl 21 to 24 cents and chicken 23 to 26 cents, while the William Davies Company were quoting 22 to 25 cents for fowl and 25 to 27 cents for chicken, and right through to September they were charging more than other companies, and he recommends that the cold storage plant should not be permitted any longer to carry on business in that way, and he criticises severely the fact that this [DOT]enormous quantity-perhaps not enormous, it is 35 tons or more of very excellent and delicate food needed in the country at that time of the year-was allowed to deteriorate and had to be thrown into the dump, and says that it should not be allowed to hap-[DOT] pen again.
In conclusion, I must say that this .gentleman who is at the head of these
great operations should not be allowed by the Government to go along any further having such power and control over these matters as he now has. Sir Joseph's power of spending is one million dollars a day, over three hundred millions a year, of the money of the people of Canada. His conduct in his own private business, his greedy profiteering, his defiance of public sentiment, his outraging of public opinion, do not make him a fit custodian and spender of this vast sum of the people's money, nor can the Government of Canada retain the confidence of the people when a thrice-convicted war profiteer and food hoarder is kept in the powerful position which he at present occupies. Surely the people have paid a sufficient price for the services of Sir Joseph Flavelle. He parades-the fact that he works without salary, but he demanded as the price of his services not only a tribute to his bacon factory, not only a knighthood, the ordinary reward of public service, but -a hereditary baronetcy, .against the establishment of which in this democracy the people of Canada very properly rebel. The " pork barrel " in politics is an Americanism which is not required in Canada, and the time is long past due when this baronet with the conscience, which " has no qualm " should be retired from public life, and the Prime Minister of Canada should so intimate to the Imperial authorities, who, no doubt, would be only too glad of a reasonable excuse to conform.
A very small part of the operations of this concern has been in this way brought before the House, and particularly before the Government,-and I trust such steps will be taken as will prevent any further profiteering at the expense of the good people of Canada. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that it is only necessary to bring this matter to the notice of the Minister of Labour and the Government to insure that such steps will be taken as will for ever put an end to any man having power to conduct his business in such a way as to unduly rob the poor people of the country of the food which should go to the sustenance of themselves and their children. It does not contribute at all to the high standing of the Government, or to the efficiency of our army and navy, or to anything that is being done in connection ,with militarism in this country, if it is for one moment believed that there are men who have backstairs and backdoor influences in connection with matters of this kind which operate to the disadvantage of the

ordinary, everyday, poor man in this country.
I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, that I was obliged to take so much time in presenting this case.

speechtext:
jMr. Speaker, I congratulate the hon. gentleman (Mir. McKenzie) on making the *longest speech which we have heard during the course of this debate. I regard this as the more remarkable because when commencing hie speech he gave some very weighty advice to the member for Queen's, P.E.l. (Mr. Molsaac) who preceded him. Perhaps the hon, gentleman thinks that the fact that he read for 'two hours out of the three during which he addressed the House will take something from the length iof his speech. However, I will say nothing further with regard! to that.
I wish to congratulate the Acting Minister of Finance (Hon. A. K. Maclean) for *the able manner in which he presented his Budget to the House and for the firm way in which he has grappled with the tremendous financial problems that confront the country. The record of the Finance Minister and of this Government in the financing of the country's affairs during the war, in the splendid loans' which they have floated, in the well-placed taxation which they have effected, is one of which they may justly he proud. The people of Canada have reason to he proud of their splendid response to the call for subscriptions to war loans, of the manner in which ordinary business affairs, of the country have been carried on, and of the wealth which has* been produced throughout the land. !We can look with satisfaction upon our financial position, and we can feel that no matter how long the struggle may last we shall be able to keep up in the collar; we shall be able to maintain the position we now occupy until that victory comes of which we are assured.
While our position is an excellent one, we should not lose sight of the fact that at

the end of Mlarch of this year our national debt is approximately $1,200,000,HOO. What that debt will be When the war is over no one can say, but if the struggle continues one, two or more years, we can be certain that i't will be substantially larger than it is now. We must remember also that in addition to our current expenditures and capital outlays, we have to make annual payments out of revenue by way of interest on our national debt, which to-day is estimated at approximately $50,000,000, and which will increase as our debt increases. Moreover, we have to meet annual payments by way of pensions, for which in the Estimates of this year some $15,000,000 are being asked. It is safe to predict that when the war ends the amount payable for pensions will exceed $50,000,000 a year.
We should have regard to two things in considering this Budget: first, the manner in which we shall raise funds during this and possibly the next year; second, the financial position in which our country will be placed at the termination of the war. To-day we have an opportunity of greatly influencing that post-war condition. In discussing this matter I wish to keep that second point more especially in view.
For many years it has been the policy of this country to rely upon customs revenues for the means to meet ordinary expenditures. I shall not make any comment upon the merits of that source of revenue, except that in time of war we must without question continue it. But our reliance upon this source of revenue should not blind our eyes to other possible means of . raising money; in the circumstances existing to-day, it is desirable that every possible source of revenue should be carefully investigated and, if deemed advisable, taken advantage of by the Government.
The other great form of taxation is direct taxation, of which in England the most important factor is the income tax-and it should be the case in Canada. Income tax has existed in England since the year 1799, when it was put on by Mr. Pitt to raise moneys for the prosecution of the Napoleonic wars. Since that date, and more especially since the repeal of the Corn Laws, that tax has been the mainstay of each Chancellor of the British Exchequer, and in England to-day that tax, more than any other source of revenue, is enabling England to carry on the war and to pay as substantial an amount as 17 per cent of its war indebtedness. They can do that in England better than

we can, do, it here because they have been accustomed to income tax for one hundred years. It is proper that in Canada we should introduce new modes of taxation slowly; no important departure in the way oi taxation should be made suddenly. Our people should be gradually educated to a new form of taxation, and only when they have accepted it can it be considered successful. What is the history of income tax in this country? The subject was discussed early last session. The Minister of Finance stated: at first that an, income tax would not be introduced-he pointed out various objections, to it-but later, towards the end of the last Parliament, the income tax which is now on our statute book was brought in. The imposition of that tax was in itself a great step forward, and after sax months we can feel that it has been favourably accepted iby the people. They have looked into that tax; they have considered the rating under it, and viewing the matter in relation to the requirements of the country, they feel that it is a tax which they should be called upon to pay. That being the case, we should consider whether or not it is advisable to make any substantial increase in the rate payable under that tax. That brings ue to the changes proposed in the tax as outlined by the Acting Minister of Finance. I agree with him in the lowering of the minimums of exemption in the case of unmarried men to $1,000 and of married men to $2,000, and the placing of the rate of 2 per cent on the amounts by which these minimums have been respectively reduced.
I feel that is only fair, and especially that those unmarried men, although not earning a great deal, should be called upon to pay some little part-I believe the tax amounts to about $10,-so that they will feel that they are citizens of this country; that they have responsibilities, and that they are taking their fair part in this war. The next important point in regard to this change in the tax is that it affects a very large number of people, and, as a consequence, a substantial revenue will be received. No one, I believe, can take exception to the exemption of $200 granted in the case of each child. A similar provision has for some time existed in the American and British Acts, and this provision will tend to make the Act a great deal more fair, and as an Act 'becomes more fair, so will it become more popular, and so will the people of Canada become more willing to pay it.
I cannot say that the surtax which is proposed to be imposed by the Government,
has impressed me as have the other two items. I do not know for what reason this tax has been imposed in this manner. As I understand it, this surtax is a tax upon the super tax already imposed, and it varies in degree as the incomes become greater. I do not, however, think that this surtax is substantial. It commences with a tax of 5 per cent on the tax already assessed under the old Act, and a tax of 5 per cent on the former tax is, in my opinion, not substantial, and I cannot see that it makes any great difference in the Act.
Speaking of the classes who should be exempted, I put out in a more or less tentative manner this idea, that while possibly those who are serving in His Majesty's forces and navy should not be entirely exempted from the operation of this tax, some exemptions, greater than those ordinarily given, should be granted to them, because I think it is evident to every one that, in most cases, those who are overseas are not receiving as much as they were heretofore receiving, or as much as they would to-day he able to earn in this country. If by sending them overseas we have taken away a source of income from them, then to that extent they should he exempted from the operation of this tax.
Leaving, however, those points which are more or less smaller points in this subject, I come to the next change which has been proposed by the minister. That is the very heavily increasing taxation on incomes over $50,000. To this I can only most heartily agree and say that I personally would he willing to go considerably further in regard to those increases. There is another great class of incomes in which no change has been made. There are large incomes, underneath the sum of $50,000. per year which are not very heavily affected by the present tax. iln order that I may present this matter definitely, I shall lay before the 'House a table showing what the tax on incomes between $5,000 and $50,000 would be if the rate were doubled. This will be in the case of a married man without children, premising that the exemption would be $2,000, and that the rate between $2,000 and $3,000 would be one-half of the normal tax. This is the table:
Income.	Tax.	Net Income.$ 2,500	$ 20	$ 2,4803,000	40	2,9604,00!0	120	3,8S05,000	200	4,8006,000	280	5,72010,000	760	9,24020,000	2,5.60	17,440
I have read these figures to the House because I think they will show that even m the lowest income, for example, that of $2,500, the payment wtould be only $20. I do not think that could be considered as being too heavy a drain upon the individual, nor one which he could not well afford to pay. As we get up into the higher amounts, for example, an income of $20,000, 1 d'o not think the sum of $2,560 would be a tax which that man could not, having regard to everything in this country,. pay, and I think that the balance of $17,440 should be sufficient for him to maintain himself upon each year. The first point I want to make is that I feel that the rate under the income tax should generally be substantially increased, and that especially the higher incomes should be very substantially taxed. I believe, upon the figures which I have just given to the House, showing the effect with the rate doubled, it is apparent that each person should be able to afford the tax which he would have to pay and should have quite sufficient left to maintain himself in the degree of comfort to which he has been accustomed. If any further evidence should be required as to the possibility of a family having an income of $2,500 being able to afford a tax ci $20 and to live on a net income of $2,480, I should like, for purposes of comparison, to draw the attention) of the House to a large class of families living to-day in Canada. Every hon. member has met with them in his constituency. I refer to the families of soldiers overseas who are living on the moneys which the Government and the Patriotic Fund give to them. We all know the sort of life that some of those families have to lead. We know they have nothing but the bare necessities of life. I believe $15 is the amount of the assigned pay, $25 the amount of the separation allowance, where there are no children, and the amount donated by the Patriotic Fund varies. Think for a moment of the amount on which those families are living, and they comprise no inconsiderable proportion of the people of this country. Some
400,000	men have enlisted, and from that we can deduce the number of families in our country who are living on that scale. Personally, I believe the amounts payable to those families should be increased; but I am using this illustration to show the possibility of a family living on a less income than it now receives. I quite agree" with the statement that a tax to be successful must be popular. I believe the people of Canada would accept a very substantial increase in the income 
tax, and the more readily because the strain of war is upon them. Our people are interested in the war more than in any other question which could possibly come before them, and for that reason I think they would not object to the payment of this additional tax. It may be urged that the cost of living is higher, but on the other hand money is freer and wages in a great many, if not the majority of cases, are higher.
Another reason why I think the tax should be increased ruow is that we are having wha't might be termed a period of prosperity to a certain extent caused by war conditions, and I think we should collect for the purposes of the war a substantial portion of the money that has been made by reason of the war. I am not advocating any vfery drastic tax. I do not think the figures I have given could be considered drastic. Another reason why I think we should increase this tax now is lest our people might get the idea that the tax will never be increased, that the present tax is fixed and furnishes a precedent. If the time is ripe, and I think it is, we should move up logically to the next step.
Referring to the collection of the income tax, the Minister of Finance last session stated that one great objection to such a tax in this country was the vastness of our territory, compared to our population, which made its collection difficult, but that objection is eliminated as regards the increased tax I am proposing, because we already have our collecting system established, and it would cost very little, if anything, more to collect a higher i;ax.
Let us consider what would be the result to the finances of this country if the present income tax were doubled or trebled, and if higher rates were assessed on the bigger incomes. The Acting Minister of Finance, in introducing this tax, estimated it would yield between seventeen and twenty million dollars, and I do not think any public ^statement has been made in reference to that estimate since. Taking that as our basis, and premising the doubling or trebling of the rate and increasing the assessment on higher incomes, we could hope to obtain in this way a sum between fifty and seventy-five million dollars. I believe this amount is required in this country to-day. It is true we are paying our current expenditure, and still have some surplus to apply on our post-war indebtedness. It is all a question of the extent to which we should go >n the imposition of taxes, in the reduction of our

indebtedness, and in the amount of indebtedness we are justified in leaving to the future. I believe the amount realized from this tax, together with the surplus which we now appear to have from year to year, would enable us to reduce our war expenditure by at least one hundred million dollars a year, and I do not think we should set our ambitions at anything lower than that. England in the years 1916 and 1917 paid off 17 per cent of her war expenditure, and she did that almost entirely by direct taxation, for she has not, relatively speaking, any customs revenue. England has [DOT]done that while she is fighting with her back to the wall, while she can hear the guns of the enemy thundering across the channel. In view of the great strain and financial demands upon them and theii proximity to the wrar, it is astounding that the people of England have been able to pay off as much as 17 per cent of their war expenditure. The Americans are arranging to pay off 14 per cent, and while it is a matter for congratulation that we in Canada have paid off 11 per cent, I know of no Teason why Canada should not do as well as England and the United States, and I feel that this is possibly the easiest and most proper way to raise the money required to retire annually such a substantial portion of our war indebtedness.
It may be said by some, that if we impose such a severe tax it would interfere with our war loans. I quite agree that the major portion of the money we require to carry on this war must be obtained by means of war loans, but I do not think the imposition of this tax would interfere with the success of the war loans. After all, while the sum is substantial in itself, it is not very great for each individual, nor is it very great in comparison with the amount w'hich we may have to borrow. To take care of our war needs, the next loan may have to be for $400,000,000. I do not think the imposition of this tax would cause our people to subscribe less freely to the war loans, or decrease to any appreciable extent the funds 'which they would have to subscribe.
One thing at least is clear. By the imposition of this tax we should reach a class of our people who do not now subscribe to war loans, and who tout for the imposition of some such tax as this will never contribute to this war. From one end of our country to the other there is scattered a class, small, it is true, who for different reasons are not contributing to our war
loans, and this is the only manner in which they can be made to do their share.
I might suggest this further idea. If it is apparent to our people that their incomes will be substantially taxed for war purposes, and if we continue to make our war loans free from income tax I should imagine the imposition of this tax would incline people more and more to the purchase of war loan bonds. Whether we should issue our war loans free of income tax, is a very important 'question. In order to influence people gradually to buying loans subject to income tax, an option might be given to purchase bonds at par, [DOT]if they want them free of income tax, or [DOT]at something less than par if they are to be subject to the income tax. A gentleman suggested that to me in conversation to-day, and it is a possible mode of making the transition from loans free of income tax to' loans subject to the tax. Personally, I do not think this tax would have any bad effect on the war loans, and I certainly think it should be imposed. I think that all we have to do is to grasp this question firmly and put it through. I believe that we will find that this tax will be popular, that our people will pay it without complaining and that they will rise to the necessities of the situation by purchasing war (bonds as they did (before.
Soane people may object to the 'increase of this tax because they fear that our people, or their money to some extent, may emigrate to the United States. One can only estimate what the effect of a substantial increase in this tax may be in that regard. I can. only say in the light I have been able to obtain with regard to the question that I do not believe that such a result as this will be brought about. Eventually our indebtedness must be paid. The United States are perhaps, in some regards, not in as good a condition as we are with reference to the financial side of our war operations. We are further on in the war than they are; we know where we are; we know how much we must provide, what we have to provide for and what our expenses are. On the other hand the United States are practically commencing. They do not know what their, costs will be and' they do not know exactly the form o<f taxation which it will be advisable for them to im-po.se. So, I cannot see any great force in any comparison which might .be made if we should raise the rates of taxation in this country higher than those which exist in the United States. While that may be true with regard to emigration to the United



States, unless we substantially decrease our national debt that may aot as, a great de-terent to immigration into this country. We should endeavour to, so reduce our national delbt that after the war Canada can be looked to by the prospective immigrants as a country which, if it has not a proportionately less debt has no greater defb't than other countries which may be offering inducements to immigrants. Having regard to our great need of immigration after the var, the problem of the amount of our national debt will be an important factor, and we should endeavour to grapple with that problem now as firmly as we can. When the war is completed we will require a large amount of money to develop the resources of the country, to. carry on until they become more productive our railways to assist our returned soldiers and to promote those more or less co-operative enterprises which are creeping into our national life. We shall be very seriously handicapped if, at the end Of the war, we have made no substantial progress in redeeming an appreciable part of our national debt.
I do not believe that the imposition of this tax will tend to discourage or disorganize business in any manner. It may be true that the business profits war tax- that is, the tax on business itself-if carried too far, might discourage initiative and enterprise among business men. hut it -must be remembered that this income tax is not being levied on business itself, where perhaps some surplus is required for the purpose of new enterprises and expansion, hut it is being levied on money that is free even from the control of business organizations. It is not being taken away from any particular business. It is being taken from the moneys of individual people throughout the country and I do not see that there is any great danger of discouraging initiative or enterprise or harming business in any way. This is perhaps the feature of greatest importance that we must consider in imposing any tax. I feel personally that there is no substantial reason why the rate of this tax should not be doubled or even trebled and why incomes in the higher amounts should not he even more heavily assessed than they appear tc he in the Budget which has been brought down. I have not been able to discover any good reason why this should not be done and I feel personally very strongly that it should be done. I think that I have made out an economic case for increasing substantially the rate of this tax. There is another feature and that is that [air. Redman.]
this tax would act in the nature of an equalizer in the matter of sacrifice in this country. A large proportion of our people were called upon to go overseas, to work for $1.10 a day, to endure hardships and to run the risk of losing their lives, many have lost them. At home their families are living on the bare necessities. These men are not able tfo take advantage of the economic prosperity here as many of us who remain at home have been able to. We are enjoying all the conditions which we would have enjoyed in peace time. In addition, we are enjoying even greater prosperity than ordinarily exists in peace time. I have been very closely in touch with a large portion of those who are serving overseas ever since the outbreak of the war, and I think I can indicate to the House what their feelings are. They have a right to express their feelings in regard to this matter, and they feel that while they are doing these things for us we should sacrifice something ourselves. We should sacrifice something out of the money we are making and which we can well afford to part with. It seems to me that when our fellow Canadians overseas are endeavouring to defend us against the German onslaught we might he called upon to protect and defend this country against any burden of excessive debt or any possibility of bankruptcy. Therefore, I believe this measure will be an equalizer or sacrifice, and I believe further that those of our people who remain at home and who have not been called upon as yet to make as great a sacrifice as have the soldiers, wish to do their fair share. This tax will not be unpopular. On the contrary, it will be popular. I believe that the people expressed themselves on, that point at the last election, and that it was their intention, and their mandate to the Government to increase the taxation as well as to obtain the necessary men. For the reasons I have given, more especially for the economic reasons, I recommend that the question of substantial increases in the rates under the Income Tax Act, should receive the most careful consideration of this House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like every member of the House and many taxpayers outside, I was very much interested in the Budget speech as brought down by my hon. friend the Acting Minister of Finance. I appreciate that at a time like this it is a very difficult matter to produce a Budget that will meet with the approval of every one. In this

time of stress and trouble in Canada it is particularly hard, but I believe that it is our duty, not only in connection with the Budget, but' in connection with any legislation that may be brought down, to have 'but one thought in mind, and but one object- in view: that is to enact such laws as will best assist our country and the Empire at the preseht time. Any criticism that I may have to offer will be absolutely with that object in view and animated by that spirit.
I feel that the Government are deserving of particular credit for their Order in Council permitting the introduction of tractors free. Anything that will tend to increase production in Canada at the present time will be of real assistance to the Allies and of real assistance to the country. I only regret that the Government do not see their way to going further and absolutely eliminating the duty on all farming implements. Personally I stand, always have stood, for a tariff for revenue purposes, but as has been well said by various hon. gentlemen, this is not the time for tariff discussion. It is rather a time when we should come to a decision to do what is best for the country; and surely no one can gainsay that what Canada needs now is greater production. If free tractors will make for greater production, surely free agricultural implements of all kinds will make for that result to an even greater extent, and I believe the Government s-honld give this matter further consideration.
So far as the Te-imposition of the Business Profits War Tax is concerned, I feel that the action of the Government will meet with the approval of the people at large. I do not agree with one hon. gentleman who said that perhaps the business interests will feel aggrieved. .My own experience of the business men of Canada, -during this war, is that they have been generous of their time, generous of their money, and even generous of their families, and I believe they will be the last to grumble with respect to any taxes *which the Government require them to pay. But, Sir, should there be men -mong them who do not desire to pay over to the Government some of the profits they are receiving at the present time, it is fitting and proper that measures should he taken that will enable the Government to collect such profits.
I quite -agree with wha-t my hon. friend from East Calgary (iMr. Redman) has said with reference to the Income Tax, and
89i
I think the proposition should receive 'the careful consideration of the Government. I believe that the men who are in a position to pay that tax should be required to pay, 'that the men who are in a position to carry the burden should be made to carry it; and the burden -should be made as *light as possible upon those who can least *afford to pay it, that jie, the forking classes of Canada. I agree with the hon. member for Calgary that if it is not too late some action -should be taken along that line.
In connection with the Income Tax, there :is a matter which affects our own locality, to which I would- be glad to call the attention of the Acting Minister of Finance, and *it is this: Living on the border, as we do in the city of Windsor, there are many of our citizens who -are employed across the river in the city of Detroit, and, vice versa, there are many citizens of Detroit who are employed in Windsor. To-day Canadians who cross 8rom Windsor to work in Detroit are subjected 'to a tax of two and a half per cent on their wages, *but there is no provision for such a tax *on American workmen crossing to our side. I do not advocate imposing a tax on American workmen coming into Canada, because I realize that in many instances their wages are not very large and they could not perhaps afford1 to pay it, but I do believe there should he some reciprocal arrangement between the two countries that -would free our people from the obligation *of paying this tax. I do not know whether *the minister has had the matter before him, but I hope that representations have been made to Washington that will enable us to bring about a settlement o-f this matter -in a manner that will be satisfactory to our people.
There is -another suggestion that I wish to offer to the minister. There may be reasons why it should not be accepted, but they do not occur to me at the moment, and that is ini connection- with the Business Profits- War Tax and the Income Tax. It would seem to me advisable, if possible, that when statements are sent in by corporations or by individuals, they should be accompanied by a cheque for the amount which is owing the Government at that time. I know of some cases-and I have no doubt there are other members of the House who know of many cases-in so far as the Business Profits Tax is concerned, dating back to 1915 that have not been adjusted. This country is a heavy borrower, and if it is possible to adjust anything that may he wrong in this statement, it is just

as easy and just as feasible to adjust it with a cheque rather than to allow the matter to drift for two or three years with the amount that is due remaining uncollected. I believe if the Finance Minister will take that matter under advisement he will probably find it will enable him to come into .the immediate possession of many millions of dollars that otherwise he anight have to w'ait for until the matters in dispute have been adjusted. I give the suggestion to the hon. gentleman for what it is worth.
J am heartily in accord with the tax that has been placed upon the packers; after listening to the statement of my honl friend from Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) tonight, 'I do not (believe there is a man in the House who will say that he is not heartily dn accord with the tax which has been placed, upon those gentlemen. My thought in connection with this matter is this: I hope that the Government of this country will not realize a five cent piece from the excess profits so far as the packers are concerned; there should be some regulation of prices in the interest of the consumer, and if this is done there will be no excess profits. I know what I am talking about, because I live in a city and I am in touch with workingmen who are earning three to four dollars a day. It is difficult for them to get along as it is, and properly care for their families, bearing in mind the high prices exacted for food, clothing, shoes, rent and fuel, without paying profits either to the packers or to the Government. It does not make very much difference to the workingman with his three and a half or four dollars a day, whether the profits go to the packer or go to the Government. In the one instance he, perhaps, gets an indirect benefit, but that benefit is not very apparent to him when he draws his wages at the end of the week and settles his bills. Therefore, I believe that, if possible, legislation should be enacted with a view to regulating prices in the interest of the working classes. I do not know whether the Food Control Board can be utilized in this connection, certainly some effort should be made to regulate food prices so that the average worker may have the opportunity to live like a white man in this country of ours.
There is one tax that I do not agree wdth, but take great exception to, and that is the tax on tea. It does seem to me that the Government could have found some other method of raising three million dollars per annum than by taxing the poor man's table

I would suggest to the Finance Minister that he take a look at the Financial Times of Saturday, April 20, 1918, where he will notice an interesting statement. It shows that $500,000,000 constituted the three-yeax profits of ninety companies, and the paper in question gives a list of the companies. Some of them were food companies, some were steel companies, and all of them will bear inspection. It seems to me that many of these companies could well have contributed the $3,000,000 that is being exacted from the people of Canada by a ten-cent tax on tea. Now, the Financial Times is a very responsible paper; it speaks for " the interests " in this country, if any paper does, and it says this:
Five Canadian steel companies: Dominion Steel Corporation, Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company, Lake Superior Corporation, Ontario Steel Products, and the Steel Company of Canada for 1917 report earnings aggregating $27,582,623, compared with $9,341,460 in 1915, being an increase of 196 per cent.
I have also before me the annual report of the Steel Company of Canada, which shows that in 1914 the profits for the year were $539,811, and in 1917, the net profits, after deducting charges for repairs, maintenance and improvements, and providing for war tax, amounted to $6,040,318. The figures which I have given might well be investigated by the Government, when perhaps the Acting Minister of Finance would find some other way of raising the $3,000,000 that he proposes to collect by a tax on tea. I have another suggestion to offer in connection with the $3,000,000, and that is that the Order in Council to control the packers should be made retroactive, thus enabling the Acting Finance Minister to go back after Sir Joseph Flavelle and his eighty per cent. If the Acting Finance Minister does that it will meet with the approval of the people, and the Government will stand high in the public estimation. Furthermore, by carrying out my suggestion they will be placing the burden where it properly belongs.
There is another matter that to my mind merits the attention of this House, a matter which concerns the whole of our people and yet seems to have passed unnoticed-I refer to the amalgamation of banks. We who have been reading the press know that very re' cently there have been two amalgamations, and we know that slowly, but surely, the number of chartered banks in this country is decreasing. During the past ten years the chartered banks have decreased from thirty-four to nineteen, and it will only be a matter of a short time until we probably

will (have in 'this country three great banking systems, perhaps the Bank of Montreal, the Canadian Bank of Commerce, and the Royal Bank. And these banks, with a couple dozen of directors, will control the finances of this country. I do not believe [DOT]that that will be a good thing for Canada. Nor do I believe that any amalgamation of banks should occur at the present time, at least until the matter is brought before the Banking and Commerce Committee and this House. We are the representatives of the people; the banks are the trustees of the people. The people place their money in the banks, and they should be under Government regulations, as they are. I cannot see why the Acting Minister of Finance, or the Governor in "^Council, should have the power to permit the amalgamation of .banks without having the matter discussed in the House. I can appreciate that under some conditions there might be necessity for immediate action to protect the depositors or shareholders, but I do not believe that under proper Government inspection there is even a remote contingency of that kind. I think the banks in this .country are strong financially, and certainly the amalgamation that tobk place the other day between the Bank of Montreal and the Bank of British North America had no justification. We, representing the (people, should have the opportunity of knowing why these amalgamations are [DOT]being made and what their object is.
You know, .Sir, that in the United States very recently-and I speak very deferentially of the United States, because I notice that hon. gentlemen opposite are giving it some thought these days and are treatr ing the United States rather deferentially too-a law was enacted, as against what they term interlocking directorates. We in 'Canada seem to be getting away from that, and we are interlocking the banks rather than the directorates. I think the time has reasonably come when the law .should be changed. Perhaps it is almost sacriligeous to say a word against the (Canadian banking system. We are told [DOT]from early morning till late at night that it is the greatest system in the world, that it makes currency elastic, that it keeps [DOT]up the credit of the country, that it is so superior that no other possible system should be thought of. I believe it is a good system so far as elasticity of currency is concerned. But, while it may be a better system than they have in the United States, the Americans seem to have worried along pretty well notwithstanding the fact that their system does not begin to compare with
ours. From my knowledge of it, I have no hesitation in saying that they seem to be pretty well satisfied with it. It does something which this system of ours does not do; it encourages the growth of smaller communities and builds up small towns and cities. Under the system in vogue in Canada, the banks, outside of two or three great centres, are simply depositories. They obtain what deposits they can, which are transferred as speedily as possible to the head offices which use them for any purpose desired. It is a well known fact that money which should have been used for the development of Canadian manufacturing and other enterprises has gone into Mexico, the West Indies, South America and even into far-off Spain;-and to Germany also, as the hon. member for Prince (Mr. Joseph Read) informs me. There is a difference between this and the American banking system. Under the American system, if a man wants a credit he goes to the 'bank, and fifteen minutes afterwards he knows whether he is to get it or not. The personality of the borrower, not always the collateral that he takes with him, is the basis of the credit. A man's character, his business ability, his record in the community, are large considerations under the American banking system. What happens under our Canadian system? When a man outside a large centre wants money, he goes to the local manager of a bank and fills out two or three forms, which are forwarded to the inspector for the district. The inspector examines these carefully and turns them over to the second vice-president, second general manager, or somebody else, who, ii the loan is large enough or of sufficient consequence, turns the matter over to the board of directors. If the directors do not want the money for some one close at home on the day in question, the man is liable to get it-but he is more liable not to get it. That is the difference between tile United States system and ours. The great New England manufacturing centres have been built up by the American banking system. In banking, as in other businesses, one requires competition. It is a mistake to permit banks to amalgamate, and I submit that no further amalgamations should *be permitted without good reason therefore being given on the floor of this House.
Since I have been in this House I have heard a great deal about what the Government have been doing; how very capable the administration has been; how glad the people ought to be because they have Union Government. May I say to hon. gentlemen

how the Victory Loan was arranged for, and that he will not do anything along the same lines, but will do something different. I do not believe that the Minister of Finance handled the Victory Loan in the proper -manner. If the Government will go out to the people of the different cities and towns in this country, they will receive the support of all the business men, who will be glad to give their time for nothing so as to help this country in this great crisis.
Mr. W. F. OOCKS'HUTT (Brantford): Mr. Speaker, I presume it is the wish of the House that the debate should he continued. I do not like to inflict myself upon the members at so late an hour as this; but if it is the wish of the House, I shall proceed, and my good frend from North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) may bear a part of the blame on account of his three and a half hour's speech.
The proposals of the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. A. K. Maclean) were very well placed before the House, and with them I am in hearty accord. I am sorry I cannot agree with the criticisms of my hon. frend from North Essex (Mr. Kennedy) with regard to the duty on tea. No fitter tax could possibly be placed on anything in Canada that is not taxed than the tea and coffee tax. That is a 'tax that touches everybody-and so it should. The war is everybody's war, and those that cannot be reached through the Income Tax, which is only for those who have a considerable income, can be reached by such minor taxes as that, and I must entirely dissent from my hon. friend in taking exception to the taxing of tea and coffee, because those are natural products that are used by everybody and are very legitimate objects of taxation. Our hon. friends opposite are very fond of quoting free trade England, as to what should be taxed and what not. Even now the tax on tea in Canada is very much less than the tax on f'ea in free trade England, and the same is true in regard to coffee and cocoa. *Therefore, my hon. frend, if he is a free trader, must say that the precedent is good when the acting minister has adopted a tax that has been in vogue in Great Britain fo.r upwards of a quarter of a .century, and which is bringing into them .million of pounds sterling per annum. In my judgment, this tax should have been imposed three years- ago. When the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) made his first Budget speech after the war *started, I told him privately that he had .missed the best opportunity of taxation I 
knew of, and that was- tea. IBe told me it would be putting a great deal of money into the pockets of tea holders, but the Acting Minister of Finance has shown that -there can be placed upon tea a tax which [DOT]is not only prospective, but .retroactive, [DOT]and it will be collected on all the teas -that are in store as well as on teas that .are now 'to be stored. This is very commendable, and the acting minister has [DOT]followed that policy with regard -to so-me other matters mentioned in his tax list. . The new taxation is moderate and judicious and cannot reasonably be taken exception- to by any of our citizens. Exception has been taken to it to a certain extent, but, I think, in a very limited way by our friends opposite who have spoken *on the question up to the present. Taxation, in all its forms, is more or less .objectionable, and no one likes to be taxed -in any way that can possibly be avoided, -but in war times such as these taxation as absolutely necessary in order that the coffers of the Government may be filled. The coffers of the .Government have been [DOT]fairly well filled during the past year, and *the Acting Minister of Finance has- been .able to 'tell us we have a surplus over ordinary expenditure of about 555,000,000.
It is true my hon. friend from Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) takes-exception to that and says there is no surplus at all if the book-keeping is properly done. He says the acting 'minister is crediting all the taxes raised for war purposes in order to .make a good showing. But in doing that he is only pursuing the policy that has been adopted by all Finance Ministers in the past, including the Finance Minister of the Government of which my hon. friend was a supporter for so many years. They all took this taxation and credited it as the Acting Minister of Finance has done on this occasion. There are those, I know, who think that the taxation should take care of pretty nearly all the cost of the war, but in my judgment that is not a well founded opinion. This is not a war of this generation alone. This war was not brought about iby the men of Canada; we were forced into it, and in my judgment it is up to posterity as well as to the present generation to pay a share of the cost of this war, and future generations will recognize that in no uncertain way; "they will admit that part of Hie burden borne by the Allied countries has justly been placed on them, and they will bear their fair share in the years to come. When the young men of this generation are going forth to fight-

and they are worth more than our money, when they are giving their life's blood in order that the future generation may be spared such a war-it is but a light thing to ask that posterity should help pay the cost of this war. I think the Finance Minister has been very wise in not attempting to pay all the cost of the war at the present, time, and I know that here I am not in accord with two or three hon. gentlemen on this side of the House who spoke yesterday. The hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Blake) stated that the people should pay the cost of the war practically as we went along; that is an impossibility, and it would be unwise for us to do it even if it were possible. This war is for future generations as well as for the present, and posterity should bear, and will be willing to bear, part of the burden that has been added to the public debt. We are giving our young men, who cannot be replaced. Capital can be replaced, either by borrowing or by production. Therefore, I say, this generation is making a sacrifice that the future generations will not ^ be called upon to make. We believe the object is worth the price. We are fighting for the liberties of the world, fighting that right may prevail, and that iniquity wherever it is exalted shall be brought low. The utmost that we can do to win the war ie what is required of us at the present time. Nothing else counts. That is the reason we have at the present time a Government that has been brought together with the object of winning the war. That brings me to a point my hon. friend from North Cape Breton made in his discursive speech of three hours and a half. He referred to me as the first man to say that there was an agreement entered into as to the formation of this Government. I was not in the House when he made that statement-I endeavoured to put in the three hours while he was speaking, but I could not put in all the time. Now 1 am not in possession of any private information that is not open to the hon. gentleman, or that has not been open to him as to any agreement or agreements that were made between the various parties composing the present Government. What I stated the other evening was* what I believed to be the truth, and what is common knowledge not only to the members of this House who take any interest in current events but to all those who read the newspapers. The newspapers have said there was an agreement by which Union Government w*as brought about. Otherwise, the Union Government could not have been brought together. This Union Government, as I understand it, ie composed of men from both sides of politics who were prepared to sink all difference and strive to win* the war; that was the one and sole purpose. ' That was declared from every platform in our part of the country, and I am sorry Cape Breton is so far from the centre of civilization and population that the hon. member did not hear of it until now. It appears our hon. friend from Cape Breton North never heard of it during the election. Up in our part of the country it was announced from every platform that that was the basis of Union Government, that all minor matters were to stand aside, that all these matters the hon. gentleman has referred to in his discursive speech of three and a half hours to-night were not to be mentioned by men on this side of the House. The one 6ole object was to win the war, believing that nothing else mattered, believing that if we lost the war we lost everything.	That was what brought
these, men	together-and all honour
to them-who, holding their opinions just as strongly as I bold mine, were prepared to lay them aside and to say; This is a special time when men are called upon to sacrifice, and we propose to sacrifice our opinions for the general good, and to devote ourselves entirely to the winning of the war and to nothing else until that has been accomplished.
