speechtext:
Nothing more dangerous to the continued existence of the Union Government could well be imagined than the injection into -parliamentary discussion at this time of the tariff issue.	*
1 commend that to my hon. friend the member for ©rome.
This fact is -recognized, not only by the more responsible members of the Union party, but by the Laurier Opposition itself. For the very reason that it recognizes this question as the most vulnerable spot in the armour of the Union party, the Opposition would welcome any introduction of the tariff issue into the deliberations of Parliament.
Only toy some such means could Laurier hope to divert to his own purposes the votes of certain ill-advised1 and short-sighted advocates of tariff changes among the Union majority-and he has no doubt hopes also of certain of the members of the cabinet itself- with a view to overthrowing the Government by s-tirring up discord over such a bitterly controversial subject.
It was well understood that above all things the tariff question was to be. shelved until after the war.
I hope my hon. friend from Gape Breton will take note of these words.	-
That was the understanding upon which the Union movement was based. In no other way could the Union movement have made any headway. Every public man who had anything to do with the negotiations which led to the formation of the Union party was a party to that understanding. It was openly discussed; it was freely published; it was authoritatively announced. On the question of whether or not there was such an agreement there can toe no doubt whatever. The agreement was understood by everybody to be in effect.
To break that agreement now would be a breach of faith, a betrayal of trust, which would be inexcusable. Not only would it he morally reprehensible, but in practice it would have the effect of destroying the unity of Union. It would result in the wreck of the Union Government. It would jeopardize the most vital interests of the nation.
Unfortunately there are Unionist members of Parliament pledged to refrain from advocating tariff alterations during the war who are to-day openly advocating and demanding those very changes.
However honest such men may toe in general, in this particular they are both dishonsst and dangerous in the extreme.
Unfortunately the Government has given a measure of encouragement to such unreliable persons toy showing a willingness to tamper with the National Policy on which Canada's successful past was -built, and on which its present and future prosperity depends.
This war has shown us as nothing else could show us the essential need of protecting and building up great industries from one end of Canada to the other. We must contiue steadily to become a completely organized and completely developed nation. We must not specialize in any one line of enterpries to the destruction of all other enterprises. We must be universal. We must become self-contained and dependent solely upon our own resources in any emergency that may face us.
The majority of the people of Canada recognize this fact. The minority, unfortunately, do not. For a generation, majority and minority have fought over this controversial subject both in and out of Parliament. Probably for years to come there will still be those who are determined to keep it within the realm of controversy. Consequently there is no pressing need to attempt to finish this domestic fight to-day.
The Union Government was elected for one purpose, and for one purpose alone-that was to win the war. All its followers were pledged to the same policy to the exclusion of all other policies. Any man so elected who undertakes to change his mind at this -late date will prove himself to he a -traitor to those electors of diametrically different views on questions of domestic policy who united on the one great patriotic policy for the -preservation of their country.
Canada is destined one day to be as great a nation as the great republic to the south. Canada will run a serious risk of missing that destiny, of ceasing to be a nation at all, if the present national trustees of her honour permit themselves to toe drawn into a domestic wrangle that will incapacitate them for accomplishing the one great thing for which they were appointed trustees.
There, Mr. Speaker, is a strong finding, and one, I think, that will carry conviction to the minds of all when they review the circumstances under which we are placed, jit was not my wish then that this tariff issue should have been raised at this time, -but I say, as one who has been attacked considerably during this debate by members, perhaps, on both sides of the House, that I feel it is my duty to stand to my guns, even if I do not have very much support. I am one of those who hold my opinion as conscientiously and as consistently, I think, as most, and whether hon. gentlemen agree with me or not, I think they will recognize that I try to be a fair fighter, and hang to my opinions when I -feel them to be right in the face of all opposition. And that is the reason I am to-day, as I have always been since I was a boy and took any part in public matters, a consistent supporter of the National Policy, or of protection to a moderate degree for the industries of Canada. I have -no apology to make for holding that opin-

ion to-day. lit has been justified now by forty years of experience. Canada has gone too far along that road of development ever again to retrace its steps and become a purely agricultural country. I *say that believing it to be absolutely true, and without any fear of successful contradiction. All men are not fit for the land; all men cannot make a success on the land; and why should my friend, who is a paper manufacturer, and I, who am more or less connected with the agricultural implement business, though having nothing whatever to do with its management, be condemned for helping in the upbuilding of the Dominion of Canada? That is what we are trying to do consistently, and we look upon a dollar produced in the factory as just as valuable as a dollar produced upon the farm. I know there are those who object to that statement, but that is our view which we honestly hold. I want to point out to gentlemen on both sides of the House that Canada to-day is no longer a purely agricultural country, that at least half its citizens, and I think a good deal more, derive their livelihood from other callings, and very nearly half our citizens are employed in factories. I am speaking now of that half of our citizens who are workers and producers. About half of them are workers in the factories of Canada.
My hon. friend from Brome, and, I think, most of those who took exception to the implement business being protected, say it is a mere handful of men that these duties are being exacted, for. To all who hold that view I say, it is not the manufacturer who, I admit, is a negligible quantity, but all his workers who must be recognized as manufacturers and as master builders. Regardless of the opinions of those who may differ from me, I believe the workers in the factories of Canada work as intelligently and as hard, and put in as many hours, too, in the year, as do those of any other calling. That may be disputed, but let me point out that they work twelve months in the year, nine hours per day; whereas the agriculturist and the outside .worker, though he puts in twelve to sixteen hours a day for a certain part of the year, has a great deal of sitting in in the winter time, while the workman has to put in just as many hours in the cold as in the heat. And, I tell you, it is the experience of many farmers who thought it was " easy money " in the city and have come in to make money in the factory, that, after putting in a few months, they have decided that the farm is hard enough for

them and who go back to the fann. The lot of the workingman in a factory is harder than out on the farm, to say nothing of the danger he has of being injured, for in the heavy industries there are accidents every day. In the big smelting industries, and those requiring intense heat, he must work in the terrible heat; he has to endure that heat in the dog days when the temperature is 80 to 90 degrees outside and 120 degrees inside. Anybody who thinks that the workingman should not have some consideration is shooting entirely beside the mark.
1 want to -approach this subject, not from the position of a few manufacturers who control the capital, but from the position of the manufacturer and all his assistants, because the man behind the gun is the man that makes the factory, and the product cannot be turned out from the factory unless you have the men, as everybody knows, We have in the factories to-day probably six or seven hundred workmen, as intelligent as any in the world, who are producing per man as much as any country in the world barring only the United States, which exceeds us by a small amount. The average product of the workman in Canada is about four times what it is for the British workman, and between four and five times what it is for the German workman. You ask how I make that out. On the basis of the amount of power that is applied behind the individual workimah, and on that Ibasi6 the horse-power is threefold what it is in the older countries of Europe. In other words, we do by machinery, what is done in the older countries by hand. Anybody can see why production will be vastly more by machinery than by hand power alone. This applies to- a very large number of the industries of Canada. The prosperity that has been experienced by the people of Canada during the war is very largely due to the fact that Canada was a manufacturing country when the war broke out, and we were in a very feeble position comparatively financially, and would have been in a very awkward position, had not our works been available for the manufacture: of munitions of war. They were promptly turned to this work, with the result that millions and millions of money have come across the water and have helped to- finance all our industries and have kept us going in a prosperous way, enabling us to lend hundreds of millions, to the Mother Country, and to pay a large proportion of our war expenditure as we go along. That has been possible because years ago we es-

tablished a protective policy and laid the foundations broad and deep to make Canada a world power. Let it not be forgotten that Canada is destined, if we manage our public affairs aright, to become a world power by reason of the variety of industries we have in our mid-st. We have immense natural resources in the forest, the mine, the fisheries and the field. Wherever you -look, we have all the resources necessary to make of us a great people. And it is too late in the day, as I said, to- think of turning back now when -we are producing in our factories about a billion and a half dollars, as we did last year. In point of value, exports of products of the factory vastly exceeded those of products of the farm. Does the member for Brome object to that statement? I believe it to be absolutely true.
i Mr. MciMASTER: Would this year or last year be a fair period for the making of a comparison between exports of agricultural products and those of the factory?
Mr. COCK811UTT: No; I admit the force of what my hon. friend says-a large amount of this export has been possible because of the war. But if we had not laid, broad and deep the foundations, of our industrial institutions while peace was with us, we should -not have been able to take care of this war business. We had the plants, the resources, the enterprise, the skilled Avorkmen-all that made it possible to produce what wTe produced last year, about i$l,500,000,000 worth of goods, a large amount of which was exported to the Mother .Country to help win the war. Exports to the Mother Country up to March 31, 1917- .the figures for 1918, which I have not before me, are considerably larger- amounted to $790,000,000, a large portion of which consisted of munitions. This export has helped to sustain the Mother Country in her hour of need, and it speaks volumes for the industry, intelligence and enterprise of our people and the extent of the .accumulation of capital in our. industries. / I do not know why a man should he (blamed because he has. been successful. (A-s long as a man is losing money and his business is going to the dogs, he escapes criticism; hut the moment he begins to *make money, show enterprise, diring about development, people say:	let us get after
that fellow and put him out of business; he is making too much money. We had .the spectacle last night of the member for Prince, P.E.II. (Mir. Joseph Read) asking that new duties be placed on lead, simply because he had a son in that business somewhere in British Columbia; and at the same time calling for the pulling down of an industry that it has taken thirty years to build up. .In- other words, the is prepared to throw away the successful work of thirty years and to start a new enterprise, such as- the smelting of lead, (because his son in British Columbia thinks it would be a good thing and asks him to endeavour t-o bring it about.
The member for Brome is an intelligent man and an acquisition to the House-I say this without flattery. I have had the pleasure of meeting him in committee work on different occasions, and have looked upon his opinions as being very valuable. The hon. gentleman paid particular attention to what he considered my own business. He probably does not know that personally L have nothing whatever to do with the management of any agricultural implement business or the fixing of the prices of agricultural implements. I am simply a shareholder who has long since retired from an active part in the management of a business. The hon. gentleman quoted from some remarks of mine which he said he had been carrying around in his pocket. I deem it a high compliment to me that he should carry my remarks for months in his pocket. If he wants to be an intelligent statesman. I do not know that I can recommend him to a higher authority, especially if he is studying matters pertaining to the tariff. I am glad that the hon. gentleman, who has been in the House only a short time, should have discovered that I made a speech on this subject six years ago, and that he has taken part of his inspiration with respect to the policy which he has propounded, from the remarks which I made on that occasion. I feel it my duty to myself and to those who are looking to me for information that I should make my own defence in my own humble way with regard to any connection that I have with the implement business and show exactly what that business is and has been and what it hopes to be in the future.
In the Canadian Almanac for 1918 I find that the tariff on "implements, agricultural (wheeled), operated by hand power for use as seed drills, cultivators and .ploughs," is: British preferential, 121 per cent; intermediate 17£ per cent; general, 20 per cent; while the duty on implements not otherwise specified as above is 15, 221 and 25 per cent. In addition to that, there is a war tax of 71 per cent. I do not know that this is considered a very excessive duty. In the old reform days, a tariff for

revenue only of 20 per cent was looked upon as moderate; not until that rate was exceeded was there talk of protection for special industries. I do not think, therefore, that my hon. friend can reasonably make complaint with regard to the amount of duty charged upon implements.
To all who have criticised the implement business in this country, I say that that business occupies as high a position in Canada as any other industry, and that agricultural implements are sold in Canada of as good a quality and as cheaply, excepting only a few sold in the United States, as those placed on the market in any other country in the world. The member for Brome, who is giving me an attentive hearing, will, I am sure, agree with me in that respect. I am aware that the farmer chafes under this duty and is asking for relief. The Government endeavoured to grant him a little relief-it was a small mistake on the part of the Government, but I look upon it as a serious mistake in principle-when they took the duty off farm tractors. Within twenty-four hours after that action had been taken my protest was on the way to Ottawa. I do not know whether anything of that kind will occur again, but I hope not, because that is not what this Government was elected for, and it cannot be looked upon as a war measure. If the Government removed the duty from agricultural implements, not one additional bushel would be added to Canada's production during this time of war, nor would the slightest reduction in price be effected in respect of any article of food by reason of the removal of that duty. All manufacturers- not only those of agricultural implements- in sending out their price lists, have regard to the cost of production. The cost of production is the keystone to the selling price, and to that is added a fixed amount of profit which varies in different indusrties from 10 to perhaps 50 per cent. The member for Brome will agree, I think, that the cost of production should he the basis of the price. But when we come to compare that with agricultural produce, the argument is thrown altogether aside.
I only regret that my hon. friend from Kent (Mt. MeCoig) is not in his seat. I wanted to hand out a small bouquet to him. I look upon him as a " seven by nine " statesman, that is, a man of very narrow breadth who cannot see beyond the water-ditches of his own county either in peace or war. Yesterday that hon. gentleman made an attack on the implement men
[(Mr. Cockshutt.]
*who are just as good and stand just as high in the community as does my hon. friend. I want to ask him: What about the price of beans? Let him tell us what he charges for his beans, and we will give our prices on agricultural implements. He accused a company of which he says I am a member-he used my name very freely- of advancing their price 25 per cent over others, and he quoted a firm in St. Thomas manufacturing ploughs-and he will excuse me, 1 hope, if I say that I never heard of them before. Upwards of 75 per cent of the ploughs manufactured in Canada are manufactured in the city of Brantford. They are not made by the Cockshutt firm alone, but by other firms in that city, and we think we have the business down to a science. Since the National Policy was introduced, the price of those implements has been more than cut in two. That is something to say, but the hon. member for Kent who pointed out such terrible overcharges with regard to agricultural implements, is prepared to sell for seven or eight dollars a bushel beans that cost $1 to $1.25 in pre-war days. I have bought hundreds of bushel,S' of them myself for that price.	The same is true in, regard to hie com. Let imy hon. friend look to hie own in, the county of Kent before he begins, to thrash the manufacturers of agricultural implements. We would think that we were robbing the people were we to ask the advances that his people-and I understand he is in the business-lare making out of their beans and pork. We base selling prices entirely upon the cost of production, that is the basis upon which our sales are made. But the cost of production has nothing to do with my hon. friend who sells for $8 a bushel his beans that ©an probably be pro-duced-now in war times for $2. He charges $8 a bushel because the people must have them. Let him hand out his prices. If we were to listen to my hon. friend from Kent we would think he was a man who got along on about five per cent profit.
My hon. friend from Brome (Mr. Mc-Master) will excuse me for diverting for a moment to Kent, but I think that when I am called in question as I was by the hon. member for Kent yesterday as being the author of an outrageous charge that, he says, is being made on the people of this country, I have reason to resent an imputation that would mean I am excessively desirous of taking more profits than would be justifiable under the circumstances. I have endeavoured to bear my share of this war like a man. I have been

called upon to make sacrifices. One of my friends, the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. J. F. Reid) read a pronouncement from the United Farmers. It certainly made a strong appeal to my mind and heart, especially that part where the hon. gentleman said that df I would only beg of this Government to remove the duties the United Farmers would! wish me .a place in everlasting bliss. I presume if the United Farmers control the portals of everlasting bliss, they probably also have the keys of the bottomless pit, and I am not sure, if they can consign me anywhere at all but that I shall have a better chance of the latter place than the former. My hon. friend, I am sure, desired to make that appeal to me in all frankness. I have said that personally I should be very glad to make the sacrifice in order that I might retain the good opinion of my fellows, but I am not the personification of agricultural implements; I am only a private individual of like flesh and blood with yourselves, the owner of a few shares in a manufacturing company which makes some of those implements. Although I am often charged with being the high priest of implement exactions, I am not the mouthpiece of those implement manufacturers. But I say freely that rather than have the reproaches that I have had to bear in this House from my fellows whose good opinion I do value, I would long ago have gone out of the business. Nevertheless, I think if I had been conducting a liquor business or something of that kind, I would not have been nearly so much persecuted as I have been with regard to my attachment to implements. I do not know whether it is really so serious an offence to be connected with an industry of this kind. We have endeavoured to manufacture good agricultural implements that have won a place in the markets of the world, and we are endeavouring to distribute them throughout the Dominion of Canada in a fair and proper way at reasonable prices considering the quality of the goods. I cannot say more than that. If the House, in its wisdom, is going to remove the duties on agricultural implements and run the risk of destroying all that business, it is going to jeopardise a great many million dollars' worth of capital and turn out of work a large number of industrious men who have spent their whole lives in the development of this industry. Let me tell the hon. member for Brome that -such an action would hit probably from fifty to a hundred subsidiary industries that contribute the raw material of which the implements are tnadte.
I know he dealt a little with that subject, but seemed to think my figure© were grossly exaggerated. It will touch all manner of things^-iron, steel, nuts, bolts, screw©, dieis, cotton, varnish, dyestuffs, malleable iron, paints, and a multitude of other items that go into the construction of an agricultural implement, all of which articles are more or less manufactured in Canada. Let every hon. member remember that. If you gave us a reduction in the duties we pay on imported raw materials, and if we imported those goods, we would take all that trade away from the subsidiary manufacturers of Canada. I think my hon. friend will follow me in that, and I want him to follow me, because that is an important part of the situation.

speechtext:

He gets that out of the way, and then he looks around for another industry, .and makes an attack on that. Let my hon. friend remember that binder twine was bowled out in that way. Eleven or twelve factories were put out of business at a stroke of the pen. The result was that binder twine became almost unobtainable in the West; that is a matter of common knowledge, and even to-day the supply of binder twine is very unsatisfactory. Take the case oif barbed wire, an article that used to be manufactured in scores of factories in Canada. Barbed wire was suddenly put on the free list, and we have not had a pound manufactured in Canada since, not even during the war. Why not? Because the factories were put out of business long ago by the removing of the duty. I am not finding fault with that-let by-gones be bygones-I am simply pointing out the result. You wipe out capital, put men out of business, destroy a valuable industry, and then in war time an essential industry like that is lacking. Free-trade Britain has wakened up lately to the fact that she had allowed Germany to take away many of her fundamental industries, and now when she wants these products she cannot get them at any price, and she has had to begin all over again to produce them. That is a deplorable state of things. I want every hon. member to realize that Canada is laying the foundation for a future great nation, and in order to have a. great nation you must have a division of labour and different kinds of labour; and the tariff and industry are the only ways to produce the variety of labour into which our citizens should enter and will enter. Every man is not cut out to go on the farm, and I do not know why it is argued that everybody ought to be driven to the farm. I have heard farmers say that. If a farmer was talking about going into the plough business, I would certainly advise him against it, as a friend of the farmer and of the plough business. Farmers who-would drive city men out to the farm would only be making more competition for themselves. . More stuff would be produced and it would bring prices down.
. So it seems to me a very short-sighted policy for the farmers to adocate the driving of men hack to the land. It Would cut the prices down to where the .stuff could not safely be produced, except in Prince Edward Island, where my hon. friend told us last night they could produce potatoes that DMr. Cocksf.utt.]
beat the world at twenty-five cents a bushel; if that is so, all success to them, and if the farmers think the policy I have alluded to is the best to pursue they are certainly welcome to advocate the driving of men back to the land. I have tried to farm a bit myself in the last ten years, and in many cases it has cost me more- than two dollars to raise a dollar's worth of produce.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: The hon. member is an agriculturist, not a farmer.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: And yet I am producing more food than my family is able to eat in a year, so I am doing a little bit indirectly, even if I lose in the operation. But it is making more competition for the farmer, and if I am as successful in farming as I have been accused of being in the implement business I shall get into hot water all round. I must confess that I have found the little bit of experience I have had on the farm most interesting. I look upon a dollar produced from the land as worth any five dollars I can make in the city, and I appreciate it more. It will not buy any more, but it gives you a feeling of satisfaction to have it in your pocket. A dollar made on the farm gives you a tremendous amount of satisfaction, and I for one am only too glad to see the farmers so prosperous. I do not begrudge them these high prices, but I want them to remember that they are getting high prices, and that the price of farm products is higher than the price of any manufactured goods that I know of in proportion to the cost of production and in proportion to what prices were before the war.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: On what do you base your figures?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
On the cost of production, on the value of the land, the labour required, and the amount of money employed in the business. As I have already pointed out, I do not think it costs two dollars to raise a bushel of beans in the province of Ontario, so it looks to me not fair to find fault with the merchant or manufacturer who bases his selling price only on the cost of production. In the case of the farmer the product is sold for what it will fetch, no matter how high the price, and I ask any hon. member which seems the fairer way. It looks as if there was certainly nothing in favour of the prices charged by the agriculturists that cannot be said in favour of the prices charged by the manufacturer or the merchant.

This is a country of varied interests, and it must not be developed in a lopsided way; that is, we must have a good development of all our resources, and so far as I am able to take in the situation, I think Canada has grown satisfactorily in every direction. I am delighted to see the farmers having a good innings, and I want them to make all the money they can while the sun shines, but I do not want them to starve the Allies or our soldiers'. I want to help them in every way I can to produce more stuff, but I think the price in itself ought to 'be ah, inducement, and I think it is an inducement. But we must remember that the demands of the world are very great. I believe the West to-day is in a sounder financial position than ever before in its history. I think the farmers are well content with present conditions, and therefore I say that this agitation which has been started in this debate, and which appears to spread not only on one side of the House but on the other, is not wise. We are not doing ourselves justice in debating what are really minor issues when the great issue of the war is before us.

I think if the machinery is. not made in Canada-and I do not think it is-it would be quite proper to have the duty removed under the 'circumstances, because the industry of making munitions, is a very temporary affair, and the machinery would have to be scrapped perhaps in the very near future. So I think in that case the Government would be well advised to let it in free. But I am not advocating that as a policy; I am in favour of protecting every interest and every industry; that is my platform, and I make no bones about saying so. I am a protectionist for every class, because I believe protection is good for every class. It has been proved so in the past, and will De proved again in the future, if we are not so foolish as to destroy what we have with pains and enterprise got together in the last forty years; and I do not believe Canada will do that. The farmers in Canada,
90}
in our part of the country at all events, have time and again supported the policy which I am now enunciating, and which I think is a very safe one to follow. *
I will not weary the House any further. I have been drawn aside considerably from what I intended to say by a few interruptions, but I make no complaint about that, because it is always pleasant to be interrupted when you are speaking; it gives you a chance to get the blood circulating a little more freely. If I have spoken harshly to my hon. friend from North Cape Breton who seems to be resting quietly now, I hope he will be kind enough to forgive me for having provoked him to invite me to accompany him home. I have finished my remarks now, Mr. Speaker, and I regret having kept the House until such a late hour as this. But, I was compelled to go on.
